fact: After the mutiny on the Bounty in 1789, William Bligh and eighteen loyalists sailed a small open boat about 3,600 nautical miles to Timor.

name: Blind shark
fact: The blind shark is not blind at all; it got its name because it closes its eyelids when lifted out of the water.

name: Blob sculpin
fact: The blob sculpin is a soft, gelatinous-looking fish of the deep north-east Pacific that is often mistaken for the blobfish.

name: Blobfish
fact: The blobfish looks normal at its home depth of 600 to 1,200 metres; its famous droopy face is what happens when its jelly-like flesh is hauled to the surface.

name: Blonde ray
fact: The blonde ray is a large skate of the north-east Atlantic with pale, sandy colouring and a pattern of small dark spots.

name: Blood star
fact: The blood star is a small, slender sea star of rocky northern shores, usually a vivid orange-red, with arms much longer than its body is wide.

name: Bloodybelly comb jelly
fact: The bloodybelly comb jelly is deep red so that the glowing prey in its stomach cannot be seen by predators in the dark depths.

name: Blue angelfish
fact: The blue angelfish of the western Atlantic is a large angelfish that can hybridise with the queen angelfish.

name: Blue antimora
fact: The blue antimora is a deep-sea cod relative with a violet sheen, common on continental slopes from about 800 to 3,000 metres.

name: Blue blubber jellyfish
fact: The blue blubber of Australian estuaries has no trailing tentacles, feeding with eight stubby arms, and is fished and dried for export to Asia.

name: Blue button
fact: The blue button is a coin-sized floating colony of hydroids with a hard golden disc and a fringe of blue tentacles, often washed up with by-the-wind sailors.

name: Blue catfish
fact: The blue catfish is the largest catfish in North America, reaching over 60 kilograms, and has become an invasive species in Chesapeake Bay.

name: Blue chromis
fact: The blue chromis is a brilliant blue Caribbean damselfish that feeds on plankton in open water above the reef.

name: Blue cod
fact: The blue cod is not a cod but a sandperch found only around New Zealand, where it is the favourite catch of shore anglers.

name: Blue coral
fact: Blue coral is the only living coral with a blue skeleton, coloured by iron salts, and is the sole survivor of an ancient group.

name: Blue Corner
fact: Blue Corner in Palau is a current-swept reef wall where divers hook onto the rock to watch sharks and schooling fish stream past.

name: Blue crab
fact: The blue crab's scientific name means 'beautiful savoury swimmer', and freshly moulted ones are eaten whole as soft-shell crabs.

name: Blue devil damselfish
fact: The blue devil damselfish, a brilliant electric-blue fish of the western Pacific, is a hardy aquarium favourite with a devilish temper for its size.

name: Blue dragon
fact: The blue dragon sea slug floats upside down at the surface, eats Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its finger-like tips to fire at attackers.

name: Blue-footed booby
fact: Blue-footed boobies fold their wings and plunge-dive into shoals of sardines, and the males show off their bright blue feet in a high-stepping dance.

name: Blue-green chromis
fact: The blue-green chromis is a shimmering damselfish that hovers in large shoals above branching corals, darting in when danger threatens.

name: Blue king crab
fact: The blue king crab is a cold-water crab of the North Pacific and Bering Sea and a close relative of the red king crab.

name: Blue-lined octopus
fact: The blue-lined octopus is a small, highly venomous octopus of Australian waters whose bright blue lines flash when it is threatened.

name: Blue ling
fact: The blue ling is a deep-water relative of the cod in the north-east Atlantic that can grow longer than a metre.

name: Blue-lipped sea krait
fact: The blue-lipped sea krait comes ashore on Pacific and Indian Ocean islands to rest and lay its eggs in caves and crevices.

name: Blue mackerel
fact: The blue mackerel, or slimy mackerel, is a spotted mackerel of Australian and New Zealand waters, mostly used as bait and for canning.

name: Blue Marine Foundation
fact: The Blue Marine Foundation is a British charity set up in 2010 that campaigns for large marine protected areas.

name: Blue marlin
fact: The Atlantic blue marlin can top 4 metres and is one of the fastest, hardest-fighting fish in the sea; females grow far larger than males.

name: Blue mussel
fact: Blue mussels carpet rocky shores and sandbanks of the North and Baltic seas, anchored by tough threads they spin themselves.

name: Blue parrotfish
fact: The blue parrotfish is a uniform powder-blue Caribbean parrotfish that spends most of its day grinding sand and rock for algae.

name: The Blue Planet
fact: The Blue Planet is the 2001 BBC television series on the world's oceans, narrated by David Attenborough, and its sequel followed in 2017.

name: Blue-ringed octopus
fact: A golf-ball-sized blue-ringed octopus carries enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, and its blue rings flash as a warning when it is alarmed.

name: Blue rockfish
fact: Blue rockfish school in the water column of California kelp forests and are among the fish divers see most often there.

name: Blue shark
fact: Blue sharks cross whole oceans, with tagged individuals travelling from New England to Spain and back.

name: Blue-spotted ribbontail ray
fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray's bright blue spots warn predators that its tail carries two venomous spines.

name: Blue starfish
fact: The blue starfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is a vivid blue and can regrow lost arms; its close relative Linckia multifora can even grow a whole new star from a single severed arm.

name: Blue stingray
fact: The blue stingray of southern African waters has blue markings on its back and is a favourite of shore anglers.

name: Blue swimmer crab
fact: The blue swimmer crab has paddle-shaped back legs for swimming and is caught for food around Australia and the Indo-Pacific.

name: Blue tang
fact: The blue tang, the fish behind Dory, has a razor-sharp spine on each side of its tail that it flicks out in defence.

name: Blue whale
fact: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, reaching about 30 metres and well over 150 tonnes.

name: Blue whiting
fact: Blue whiting is a small cod relative of the North Atlantic caught by the million tonnes for fishmeal and surimi.

name: Blueback herring
fact: The blueback herring runs up rivers from Florida to Nova Scotia each spring to spawn and is hard to tell from the alewife.

name: Bluefin tuna
fact: The Atlantic bluefin tuna can weigh more than 600 kilograms and is warm-blooded, keeping its muscles warmer than the sea so it can sprint after prey.

name: Bluefire jellyfish
fact: The bluefire jellyfish is a small, bluish relative of the lion's mane that is common around the coasts of north-west Europe.

name: Bluefish
fact: Bluefish hunt in savage packs along the US Atlantic coast and will keep biting even after they are full.

name: Bluegill
fact: Male bluegill dig saucer-shaped nests in colonies and guard the eggs, while small 'sneaker' males dart in to fertilise some on the sly.

name: Bluegray carpetshark
fact: The bluegray carpetshark is a slender seabed shark found only off the east coast of Australia.

name: Bluehead wrasse
fact: The bluehead wrasse of the Caribbean can change from female to male in days, and the big blue-headed males defend spawning sites.

name: Bluespotted maskray
fact: The bluespotted maskray has a dark mask across its eyes and is often confused with the bluespotted ribbontail ray.

name: Bluespotted ribbontail ray
fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray has electric-blue spots and two venomous tail spines, and hides under table corals on Red Sea reefs.

name: Bluestripe pipefish
fact: The bluestripe pipefish is a cleaner pipefish that sets up stations on Indo-Pacific reefs and picks parasites off other fish.

name: Bluestripe snapper
fact: The bluestripe snapper, yellow with four blue stripes, schools in hundreds on Indian Ocean and Red Sea reefs.

name: Bluethroat triggerfish
fact: The bluethroat triggerfish is a small triggerfish with a blue throat, found on deeper reefs of the Indo-Pacific.

name: Bluntnose sixgill shark
fact: Bluntnose sixgill sharks have six pairs of gill slits instead of the usual five and rise from deep water at night to feed.

name: Bluntnose stingray
fact: The bluntnose stingray of the western Atlantic has a rounded snout and glides over sandy flats from Massachusetts to Brazil.

name: Boatswain
fact: The boatswain, pronounced bosun, supervises the deck crew and looks after the ship's rigging, anchors and boats.

name: Boaty McBoatface
fact: Boaty McBoatface is a yellow robot submarine that won its name in a public vote and has since made long journeys under Antarctic sea ice and deep in the Southern Ocean.

name: Bobbit worm
fact: The bobbit worm lurks buried in sand with only its jaws showing and ambushes fish at night, growing up to about 3 metres long.

name: Bobtail snipe eel
fact: The bobtail snipe eel is a stubby, dart-shaped deep-sea eel with long thin jaws, found in the dark waters below 1,000 metres.

name: Bobtail squid
fact: Bobtail squid are small, round cephalopods that bury themselves in sand by day and hunt shrimp at night, and many carry glowing bacteria.

name: Bodyboarding
fact: Bodyboarding is riding waves lying down on a short, foam board.

name: Bodysurfing
fact: Bodysurfing is riding a wave without a board, using only the body.

name: Bohai Sea
fact: The Bohai Sea is the innermost gulf of the Yellow Sea, almost enclosed by China's coast, and the sea approach to the port of Tianjin.

name: Boiling
fact: Boiling cooks fish in water at a full bubble, and it is the usual method for shellfish like lobster and crab.

name: Bolivian river dolphin
fact: The Bolivian river dolphin lives in the upper Madeira basin, cut off from the Amazon by rapids, and was declared part of Bolivia's natural heritage in 2012.

name: Bollard
fact: A bollard is a short, strong post on a quay or ship used to secure mooring ropes.

name: Bomb vessel
fact: A bomb vessel was a heavily built sailing ship carrying mortars to shell coastal forts and towns from the sea.

name: Bombay duck
fact: Bombay duck is not a duck but a lizardfish caught in huge numbers off western India, where it is dried in the open air and fried.

name: Bonaire
fact: Bonaire is famed for shore diving, and its coastal waters have been a marine park since 1979.

name: Bonaire National Marine Park
fact: Bonaire's entire coastline has been a marine park since 1979, and divers simply walk in from shore to reach its reefs.

name: Bondi Beach
fact: Bondi Beach in Sydney is home to Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, founded in 1907 and often called the world's first surf lifesaving club.

name: Bone-eating worm
fact: Bone-eating worms of the genus Osedax use acid-secreting, root-like tissue to digest the bones of dead whales on the seafloor.

name: Bonefish
fact: The bonefish is the 'grey ghost' of tropical flats, a shy, fast-sprinting fish that can strip line from a fly reel in seconds.

name: Bonito
fact: Bonitos are striped, tuna-like fish of the mackerel family; in Japan 'bonito' usually means the skipjack, seared as katsuo tataki or dried into bonito flakes.

name: Bonnethead
fact: The bonnethead is the only shark known to eat and digest seagrass, which can make up over half of its diet.

name: Bonneville cutthroat trout
fact: The Bonneville cutthroat trout is the state fish of Utah and descends from fish of the vast ancient Lake Bonneville.

name: Bony-eared assfish
fact: The bony-eared assfish is a cusk-eel from 1,000 to 4,400 metres with the smallest brain for its body size of any known vertebrate, and an unfortunate name.

name: Booby
fact: Boobies are tropical plunge-divers named from the Spanish 'bobo', meaning foolish, because they were so easy for sailors to catch.

name: Boom
fact: The boom is the horizontal pole that holds the bottom edge of a sail.

name: Bootlace worm
fact: The bootlace worm is a ribbon worm of North Sea shores; one found in Scotland in 1864 measured about 55 metres, the longest animal ever recorded.

name: Bora Bora
fact: Bora Bora is a volcanic island in French Polynesia surrounded by a turquoise lagoon and a ring of reef islets.

name: Boreal clubhook squid
fact: The boreal clubhook squid is a common squid of Arctic and subarctic waters that is eaten by whales and seals.

name: Boring sponge
fact: The boring sponge dissolves tunnels into limestone, shells and coral and lives hidden inside them.

name: Borneo shark
fact: The Borneo shark is a small, rarely seen requiem shark of south-east Asian waters, named for the island of Borneo.

name: Bosporus
fact: The Bosporus runs through the middle of Istanbul, linking the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and dividing Europe from Asia.

name: Boston
fact: Boston's harbour on the Atlantic was the scene of the Boston Tea Party in 1773, when colonists dumped tea into the water in protest at British taxes.

name: Boston Light
fact: Boston Light on Little Brewster Island was the first lighthouse built in what became the United States, first lit in 1716.

name: Botany Bay
fact: Botany Bay south of Sydney is where Captain Cook first landed in Australia in 1770, named for the plants collected there by Joseph Banks.

name: Bothriolepis
fact: Bothriolepis was a Devonian armoured placoderm fish with jointed bony pectoral fins, and its fossils are found on many continents.

name: Bottlenose dolphin
fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name using signature whistles that each dolphin invents as a calf.

name: Bottlenose whale
fact: Bottlenose whales of the genus Hyperoodon are deep-diving beaked whales with a rounded, bulbous forehead.

name: Bougainville Trench
fact: The Bougainville Trench curves through the northern Solomon Sea west of Bougainville Island, continuing the New Britain Trench, whose Planet Deep exceeds 9,000 metres.

name: Bouillabaisse
fact: Bouillabaisse is a fish stew from the port of Marseille, flavoured with saffron and traditionally made from local rockfish.

name: Bournemouth Beach
fact: Bournemouth Beach on the Dorset coast offers about seven miles of golden sand.

name: Bouvet Island
fact: Bouvet Island is the most remote island on Earth, an ice-covered volcanic island in the South Atlantic about 1,700 kilometres from Antarctica with no permanent inhabitants.

name: Bow
fact: The bow is the front of a ship or boat.

name: Bowfin
fact: The bowfin can breathe air using its swim bladder and is the only living member of a lineage dating back to the age of dinosaurs.

name: Bowhead whale
fact: Bowhead whales can live more than 200 years and use their huge heads to break through sea ice.

name: Bowie Seamount
fact: Bowie Seamount off British Columbia rises from about 3,000 metres to within roughly 25 metres of the surface and is a Canadian marine protected area.

name: Bowmouth guitarfish
fact: The bowmouth guitarfish, or shark ray, has ridges of spiky thorns over its eyes and back and looks like a cross between a shark and a ray.

name: Bowsprit
fact: The bowsprit is a spar that projects forward from a ship's bow and supports the stays of the foremast.

name: Box jellyfish
fact: The Australian box jellyfish has 24 eyes and a sting that can stop a human heart within minutes, and it is almost invisible in the water.

name: Boxfish
fact: Boxfish are encased in a rigid bony box and, when stressed, release a poisonous mucus that can kill every other fish in an aquarium.

name: Brač
fact: Brač is a Croatian island whose white limestone was used in building the White House in Washington.

name: Brain coral
fact: Brain coral grows into a dome furrowed with grooves like a human brain, and single colonies can live for centuries.

name: Braising
fact: Braising cooks fish slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pan.

name: Bramble shark
fact: The bramble shark is covered in large thorn-like denticles and is so rarely encountered that little is known about its life.

name: Brandade
fact: Brandade is a creamy Provencal purée of salt cod with olive oil and garlic.

name: Brandtaucher
fact: The Brandtaucher was a German submarine built by Wilhelm Bauer that sank in Kiel harbour in 1851, and its three crew escaped by flooding the vessel.

name: Bransfield Strait
fact: Bransfield Strait between the South Shetland Islands and the Antarctic Peninsula is named after Edward Bransfield, who charted the area in 1820.

name: Brant goose
fact: The brant is a small sea goose that depends on eelgrass; when disease wiped out eelgrass on both sides of the Atlantic in the 1930s, brant numbers crashed.

name: Brazil
fact: Brazil has an Atlantic coastline of roughly 7,500 kilometres, and the mighty Amazon river empties into the ocean there.

name: Brazil Current
fact: The Brazil Current carries warm tropical water south along the coast of Brazil until it meets the cold Falkland Current off Argentina.

name: Brazilian sharpnose shark
fact: The Brazilian sharpnose shark is a small coastal shark of the western Atlantic that is caught in large numbers by fisheries.

name: Breadcrumb sponge
fact: The breadcrumb sponge grows as crumbly yellow-green crusts on rocky shores of the North Atlantic.

name: Bream
fact: The common bream is a deep-bodied freshwater fish of European lakes and slow rivers that feeds by grubbing in the mud.

name: Brendan Voyage
fact: In 1976 and 1977 Tim Severin sailed a leather-hulled boat from Ireland to Newfoundland to show that the legendary voyage of Saint Brendan was possible.

name: Brest
fact: Brest, on the far western tip of Brittany, is one of France's two main naval bases, with a huge natural harbour opening onto the Atlantic.

name: Brig
fact: A brig is a two-masted sailing ship with square sails on both masts.

name: Brigantine
fact: A brigantine is a two-masted sailing ship with a square-rigged foremast and a fore-and-aft rigged mainmast.

name: Brighton Beach
fact: Brighton's famous beach in England is made of pebbles rather than sand and is lined by a pier that opened in 1899.

name: Brill
fact: Brill are close relatives of turbot with a more oval body and a frilled front edge to the dorsal fin.

name: Brine shrimp
fact: Brine shrimp are tiny crustaceans that thrive in extremely salty lakes and lagoons where fish cannot survive.

name: Brinicle
fact: A brinicle is a hollow tube of ice that grows downward from sea ice, as very cold, salty brine sinks and freezes the water around it.

name: Brining
fact: Brining soaks fish in salt water before cooking or smoking, helping it keep moisture and flavour.

name: Brisbane
fact: The Port of Brisbane lies at the mouth of the Brisbane River on Moreton Bay in Queensland.

name: Bristle worm
fact: Bristle worms are segmented worms with paddle-like feet fringed with bristles, and they have been collected from trench floors more than 10,000 metres down.

name: Bristlemouth
fact: Bristlemouths are tiny, glowing deep-sea fish that may number in the hundreds of trillions, making them the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.

name: Bristlenose pleco
fact: The bristlenose pleco is a small armoured catfish whose males grow a bush of fleshy tentacles on the snout; it is a popular aquarium algae eater.

name: Britannic
fact: The Britannic, Titanic's larger sister, struck a mine while serving as a hospital ship in 1916 and lies on its side at about 120 metres off the Greek island of Kea.

name: Brittle star
fact: Brittle stars snap off arms to escape predators and grow them back, and they have been seen in large numbers on the floor of the South Sandwich Trench below 6,000 metres.

name: Broad-barred Spanish mackerel
fact: The broad-barred Spanish mackerel is a fast mackerel of northern Australian and New Guinea waters, named for its wide dark bars.

name: Broad-nosed pipefish
fact: The broad-nosed pipefish lives in eelgrass of the north-east Atlantic, and the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch.

name: Broadclub cuttlefish
fact: The broadclub cuttlefish hypnotises crabs by flashing moving bands of dark colour down its arms before striking.

name: Broadfin shark
fact: The broadfin shark is a rare requiem shark of Indo-Pacific coasts and estuaries, named for its broad fins.

name: Broadnose sevengill shark
fact: Broadnose sevengill sharks have seven gill slits rather than five and have been seen hunting seals in groups off South Africa.

name: Bronze corydoras
fact: The bronze corydoras can gulp air at the surface and absorb oxygen through its gut when water is poor in oxygen.

name: Brook trout
fact: The brook trout is actually a char, with light spots on a dark background, and is the official state fish of several US states.

name: Brown chromis
fact: The brown chromis is a common Caribbean damselfish that feeds in schools on plankton above the reef.

name: Brown ghost knifefish
fact: The brown ghost knifefish makes a continuous weak electric field and uses it to navigate and communicate in the dark.

name: Brown-marbled grouper
fact: The brown-marbled grouper is a large, marbled Indo-Pacific grouper that can reach about a metre.

name: Brown meagre
fact: The brown meagre of the Mediterranean makes loud drumming and grunting sounds with its swim bladder.

name: Brown pelican
fact: The brown pelican dives head-first into the sea from 10 to 20 metres up, unlike most pelicans, which fish from the surface.

name: Brown shrimp
fact: The brown shrimp of the North Sea is caught by horseback shrimpers in Belgium and potted in butter around Morecambe Bay.

name: Brown skua
fact: The brown skua is a powerful scavenger and predator that steals eggs and chicks and robs other seabirds of fish around the Southern Ocean.

name: Brown trout
fact: Brown trout that migrate to sea come back silver and much larger, and are then known as sea trout.

name: Brownbanded bamboo shark
fact: The brownbanded bamboo shark is born with dark bands that fade with age and can survive for hours out of water on exposed reef flats.

name: Brunei
fact: Brunei is a small sultanate on the island of Borneo with a coast on the South China Sea.

name: Bryde's whale
fact: Bryde's whale is named after Johan Bryde, a Norwegian who set up South Africa's first whaling stations, and it stays in warm waters all year.

name: Bryozoan
fact: Bryozoans, or moss animals, are colonies of tiny filter feeders that form crusts and fronds, each individual catching food with a ring of tentacles.

name: Bubble coral
fact: Bubble coral inflates grape-like bladders by day to catch sunlight for its algae and withdraws them at night to feed with its tentacles.

name: Bubblegum coral
fact: Bubblegum coral is a deep-sea soft coral that grows into pink, tree-like colonies up to several metres tall, with branch tips like blobs of chewed gum.

name: Buenaventura
fact: Buenaventura is Colombia's main port on the Pacific coast.

name: Buenos Aires
fact: Buenos Aires sits on the Río de la Plata estuary, which opens into the Atlantic, and its name means 'fair winds'.

name: Bulkhead
fact: A bulkhead is an upright wall inside a ship that divides it into compartments, which helps to contain flooding.

name: Bull kelp
fact: Bull kelp grows a single long stem topped by a gas-filled float the size of a grapefruit, and can reach more than 30 metres in a single season.

name: Bull shark
fact: Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found far up the Mississippi and Amazon rivers.

name: Bull trout
fact: The bull trout is a char of cold, clean rivers in north-west North America and is so sensitive to warm water that it is listed as threatened.

name: Bullet tuna
fact: The bullet tuna is one of the smallest members of the tuna family, found worldwide in warm seas and rarely more than 50 centimetres long.

name: Bullethead parrotfish
fact: The bullethead parrotfish is one of the most common Pacific parrotfish, with a blunt bullet-shaped head and a green male phase.

name: Bullhead catfish
fact: Bullheads are small, dark catfish of North American ponds and slow rivers that can survive in warm, low-oxygen water that kills other fish.

name: Bumblebee goby
fact: The bumblebee goby is a banded black-and-yellow goby of Southeast Asian estuaries that grows to under 4 centimetres.

name: Bumphead parrotfish
fact: The bumphead parrotfish is the largest parrotfish, reaching about 1.3 metres, and rams its forehead into coral to break it up for feeding.

name: Bunaken National Park
fact: Bunaken, off Sulawesi in Indonesia, is known for coral walls that drop almost vertically into deep water right beside the shore.

name: Buoy barnacle
fact: The buoy barnacle makes its own float, a foam of cement bubbles, and drifts across the open ocean hanging beneath it.

name: Burbot
fact: The burbot is the only member of the cod family that lives in fresh water, a bottom-dwelling, eel-like fish that spawns under the ice in midwinter.

name: Burleigh Heads
fact: Burleigh Heads on Australia's Gold Coast is a classic right-hand point break below a headland national park.

name: Burmeister's porpoise
fact: Burmeister's porpoise of South America is named after German zoologist Hermann Burmeister and has a strange backward-leaning dorsal fin.

name: Burrunan dolphin
fact: The Burrunan dolphin lives in sheltered bays and lakes of southern Australia, such as Port Phillip Bay and the Gippsland Lakes.

name: Butter clam
fact: Butter clams of the Pacific North-west can hold paralytic shellfish toxins in their siphons for a very long time.

name: Butter hamlet
fact: The butter hamlet is a small yellow Caribbean sea bass, and hamlets are unusual in acting as both male and female during spawning.

name: Butter sole
fact: The butter sole is a flatfish of the north-east Pacific that lives on sandy and muddy seabeds.

name: Butterfish
fact: The butterfish of the North Atlantic coast is a small, silvery, oily fish named for its soft, buttery flesh.

name: Butterfly kingfish
fact: The butterfly kingfish is the oddest member of the tuna family, a cold-water Southern Ocean fish with big scales and a heater organ that warms its brain and eyes.

name: Butterfly ray
fact: Butterfly rays are much wider than they are long, with a very short tail, and bury themselves in sand in warm shallows.

name: Butterflyfish
fact: Butterflyfish are thin, bright reef fish that often pair for life and use their pointed snouts to pick at coral polyps.

name: Buttonwood
fact: Buttonwood grows on the landward edge of mangrove forests and gets its name from its small, button-like clusters of fruit.

name: By-the-wind sailor
fact: The by-the-wind sailor floats on the surface under a stiff diagonal sail, so whole fleets of them are blown ashore in the same storm.

name: The Pass
fact: The Pass at Byron Bay in New South Wales is a long right-hand point break below Cape Byron.

name: Cabbage head jellyfish
fact: The cabbage head jellyfish drifts in warm Indo-Pacific waters, and its frilly arms resemble a cabbage or cauliflower.

name: Cabezon
fact: The cabezon is a big-headed, scaleless sculpin of Pacific kelp beds whose eggs are poisonous to eat; the male guards them until they hatch.

name: Cabin boy
fact: A cabin boy was a young servant who ran errands and waited on the officers aboard a ship.

name: Cable Beach
fact: Cable Beach at Broome in Western Australia stretches for about 22 kilometres and is famous for camel rides at sunset.

name: Cable
fact: A cable is a nautical unit of distance equal to a tenth of a nautical mile, or about 185 metres.

name: Cabo Pulmo National Park
fact: Cabo Pulmo in Baja California saw its fish biomass rise more than fourfold within a decade after fishing was banned, a celebrated conservation success.

name: Cabot Strait
fact: Cabot Strait between Newfoundland and Cape Breton Island is named after the explorer John Cabot and is the main entrance to the Gulf of St Lawrence.

name: John Cabot's voyage
fact: John Cabot sailed from Bristol in the Matthew in 1497 and reached the coast of North America.

name: Cabral's voyage
fact: In 1500 Pedro Alvares Cabral's fleet, bound for India, landed in Brazil and claimed it for Portugal.

name: Cacciucco
fact: Cacciucco is a rich Tuscan fish stew from the port of Livorno, served over toasted bread.

name: Cádiz
fact: Cádiz, on a narrow spit into the Atlantic, was founded by the Phoenicians and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.

name: White Atlantic cadlina
fact: The white Atlantic cadlina is a small white sea slug of cold North Atlantic water that feeds on sponges.

name: Cagliari
fact: Cagliari is the capital and main port of the Italian island of Sardinia.

name: Caiman
fact: Caimans are South and Central American crocodilians that are close relatives of alligators.

name: Caique
fact: A caique is a traditional wooden fishing boat of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.

name: Cairns Aquarium
fact: Cairns Aquarium in Queensland opened in 2016 and is dedicated to the wildlife of the Great Barrier Reef and tropical north Queensland.

name: Calanus
fact: Calanus finmarchicus is a rice-grain-sized copepod so rich in oil that it is the main food of herring, mackerel and the North Atlantic right whale.

name: Caldeirada
fact: Caldeirada is a Portuguese fish stew of layered fish, potatoes, onions and tomatoes.

name: Calico Jack
fact: Calico Jack Rackham is credited with the skull-and-crossed-swords flag and sailed with Anne Bonny and Mary Read before being hanged in 1720.

name: California blue dorid
fact: The California blue dorid is a deep-blue sea slug marked with yellow, found along the Pacific coast of North America.

name: California Current
fact: The California Current flows south along the US west coast, bringing cold water and the fog for which San Francisco is famous.

name: California halibut
fact: The California halibut is a left-eyed flounder, yet nearly half of all individuals turn out right-eyed, a quirk almost unique among flatfish.

name: California sea hare
fact: The California sea hare has unusually large nerve cells, which made it a model animal for memory research that earned a Nobel Prize.

name: California sea lion
fact: California sea lions are the trained 'seals' of circuses and aquarium shows and haul out in noisy crowds on San Francisco's Pier 39.

name: California sheephead
fact: The California sheephead is a big-toothed wrasse of kelp forests that crushes sea urchins; all start life as females and the largest turn into black-and-red males.

name: California two-spot octopus
fact: The California two-spot octopus has a false blue eye-spot under each real eye and was the first octopus to have its full genome sequenced.

name: Callao
fact: Callao is the main port of Lima and handles most of Peru's seaborne trade.

name: Calypso
fact: Calypso was a former minesweeper that Jacques Cousteau turned into the floating base for his films and expeditions from 1950 until it sank in Singapore harbour in 1996.

name: Cameroceras
fact: Cameroceras was an Ordovician nautiloid with a straight, cone-shaped shell that may have been several metres long.

name: Cameroon
fact: Cameroon's Atlantic coast lies at the corner of the Gulf of Guinea, close to the volcano Mount Cameroon.

name: Camps Bay
fact: Camps Bay Beach in Cape Town sits beneath the Twelve Apostles mountain range.

name: Canada
fact: Canada has coastlines on the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans, giving it the longest coastline of any country.

name: Canary Current
fact: The Canary Current flows south past north-west Africa and the Canary Islands and helped carry Columbus's ships towards the Caribbean.

name: Canary Islands
fact: The Canary Islands are Spanish volcanic islands off north-west Africa, named not after birds but probably after dogs, from the Latin canaria.

name: Canary rockfish
fact: The canary rockfish is a bright orange fish of the North American Pacific coast that was heavily overfished and then rebuilt.

name: Candiru
fact: The candiru is a tiny, slender Amazon catfish that slips under the gill covers of larger fish to drink their blood, and is feared far out of proportion to its size.

name: Candy crab
fact: The candy crab lives on soft corals of the genus Dendronephthya and copies their pink and white colours as camouflage.

name: Canning
fact: Canning seals fish in airtight tins and has long been used for sardines, tuna and salmon.

name: Cannon Beach
fact: Cannon Beach in Oregon is dominated by Haystack Rock, a sea stack about 72 metres tall.

name: Cannonball jellyfish
fact: The cannonball jellyfish is fished off Georgia and Florida, dried and exported to Asia as a crunchy salad ingredient.

name: Cannonball mangrove
fact: The cannonball mangrove is named for its heavy, round fruit, which looks like a cannonball.

name: Canoe
fact: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double-hulled sailing canoes, settling islands as far apart as Hawaii and New Zealand.

name: Canoeing
fact: Canoeing is paddling a canoe with a single-bladed paddle, and it has been an Olympic sport since 1936.

name: Cape Agulhas Lighthouse
fact: Cape Agulhas Lighthouse in South Africa, built in 1849, stands at the southernmost tip of Africa, where the Atlantic and Indian oceans are said to meet.

name: Cape anchovy
fact: The Cape anchovy is the key forage fish of southern Africa's Benguela upwelling system, feeding penguins, gannets and predatory fish.

name: Cape Breton Island
fact: Cape Breton Island forms the northern part of Nova Scotia and is known for the scenic Cabot Trail.

name: Cape Byron Lighthouse
fact: Cape Byron Lighthouse in New South Wales was first lit in 1901 and stands near the most easterly point of mainland Australia.

name: Cape Cod Bay
fact: Cape Cod Bay is the bay enclosed by the hook of Cape Cod in Massachusetts and a feeding ground for North Atlantic right whales.

name: Cape Cod Canal
fact: The Cape Cod Canal in Massachusetts, opened in 1914, saves ships a long and dangerous trip around the outer cape.

name: Cape Disappointment Lighthouse
fact: Cape Disappointment Lighthouse in Washington State, lit in 1856, guards the dangerous mouth of the Columbia River.

name: Cape eelgrass
fact: Cape eelgrass is the main seagrass of South African estuaries.

name: Cape Egmont Lighthouse
fact: Cape Egmont Lighthouse in Taranaki, New Zealand, was moved there in 1881 from Mana Island after its first site proved unsuitable.

name: Cape fur seal
fact: Cape fur seals breed in huge colonies on the coasts of South Africa and Namibia, where great whites ambush them at Seal Island.

name: Cape gannet
fact: The Cape gannet breeds on islands off southern Africa and plunge-dives for sardines and anchovies.

name: Cape hake
fact: The Cape hake is the backbone of the South African and Namibian fishing industries, caught by trawlers over the continental shelf.

name: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse
fact: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse in North Carolina is the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States and was moved inland in 1999 to escape erosion.

name: Cape Horn Current
fact: The Cape Horn Current is a cold current flowing east around the southern tip of South America.

name: Cape Otway Lighthouse
fact: Cape Otway Lighthouse in Victoria, built in 1848, is the oldest surviving lighthouse on mainland Australia.

name: Cape petrel
fact: The cape petrel is a black and white chequered petrel that follows ships and feeds on krill and fish in the Southern Ocean.

name: Cape Point Lighthouse
fact: A new Cape Point Lighthouse was built lower on the cliffs after the Portuguese liner Lusitania was wrecked there in 1911.

name: Cape Reinga Lighthouse
fact: Cape Reinga Lighthouse marks the northwest tip of New Zealand's North Island, where Maori tradition says spirits depart for the afterlife.

name: Cape Spartel Lighthouse
fact: Cape Spartel Lighthouse near Tangier in Morocco was built in 1864 and stands where the Atlantic meets the Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Cape Town
fact: Cape Town's harbour on Table Bay faces the Atlantic, where the cold Benguela Current keeps the sea far chillier than on the Indian Ocean side of the Cape.

name: Cape Verde
fact: Cape Verde is a group of ten volcanic islands off the coast of Senegal, and many Atlantic hurricanes begin as storms passing nearby.

name: Cape Wrath Lighthouse
fact: Cape Wrath Lighthouse at the north-west tip of mainland Scotland was built by Robert Stevenson and first lit in 1828.

name: Capelin
fact: Capelin are small silvery fish that spawn on Arctic and sub-Arctic beaches in their millions and feed cod, whales and puffins.

name: Capri
fact: Capri lies off the Bay of Naples and is known for its Blue Grotto, a sea cave lit by an eerie blue glow.

name: Capstan
fact: A capstan is a rotating drum used to haul in an anchor cable or heavy rope, and sailors once turned it by walking round with bars.

name: Captain Hook
fact: Captain Hook is J. M. Barrie's fictional pirate captain from Peter Pan, whose hand was bitten off by a crocodile.

name: Captain Kidd
fact: William Kidd was a Scottish privateer who was hanged for piracy in London in 1701, and his supposed buried treasure became legendary.

name: Captain Phillips
fact: Captain Phillips is Paul Greengrass's 2013 film based on the 2009 hijacking of the container ship Maersk Alabama by Somali pirates.

name: Captains Courageous
fact: Captains Courageous is Rudyard Kipling's 1897 novel about a spoilt rich boy who falls off a liner and is rescued by Grand Banks fishermen.

name: Capybara
fact: The capybara is the largest living rodent and is a strong swimmer that can stay submerged for several minutes.

name: Caravel
fact: The caravel was the small, nimble Portuguese ship of the 1400s used by explorers along the African coast; Columbus's Niña and Pinta were caravels.

name: Cardigan Bay
fact: Cardigan Bay is the largest bay in Wales and home to a resident population of bottlenose dolphins.

name: Cardinal tetra
fact: The cardinal tetra, with red running the full length of its body, is still mostly caught wild in the Rio Negro for the aquarium trade.

name: Cardinalfish
fact: Cardinalfish are small nocturnal reef fish, and in most species the male broods the eggs in his mouth without eating until they hatch.

name: Caribbean box jelly
fact: The Caribbean box jelly lives among mangrove roots and has 24 eyes, some of which can form images.

name: Caribbean Current
fact: The Caribbean Current carries warm water west through the Caribbean Sea towards the Yucatan Channel and the Loop Current.

name: Caribbean monk seal
fact: The Caribbean monk seal was hunted for its oil and was declared extinct in 2008, the last confirmed sighting having been in 1952.

name: Caribbean reef octopus
fact: The Caribbean reef octopus spreads its webbed arms like a parachute over coral heads to trap crabs and shrimp underneath.

name: Caribbean reef shark
fact: The Caribbean reef shark is the shark most often seen on feeding dives in the Bahamas and is rarely found outside the western Atlantic.

name: Caribbean reef squid
fact: Caribbean reef squid talk with rapidly shifting skin patterns and can show one display to a mate and another to a rival at the same time.

name: Caribbean Sea
fact: The Caribbean Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic enclosed by the Antilles and Central America, and its Cayman Trough is more than 7,000 metres deep.

name: Caribbean spiny lobster
fact: The Caribbean spiny lobster can navigate home using the Earth's magnetic field, the first invertebrate shown to have a magnetic map sense.

name: Carnation coral
fact: Carnation corals are soft corals that puff up into brilliant pink, red and purple bushes at night and collapse into limp blobs by day.

name: Carnegie
fact: The Carnegie was a wooden, non-magnetic research yacht that surveyed the oceans until it exploded in 1929.

name: Carnival Triumph
fact: The Carnival Triumph was crippled by an engine-room fire in 2013 and drifted for days in the Gulf of Mexico, with passengers left without power.

name: Carnivorous sponge
fact: The carnivorous sponge of Mediterranean caves catches tiny crustaceans on hook-covered spicules instead of filtering the water.

name: Carp
fact: Common carp has been farmed for food for more than 2,000 years and is still the traditional Christmas Eve dish in Poland and the Czech Republic.

name: Carpathia
fact: Carpathia, the ship that rescued Titanic's survivors, was itself torpedoed and sunk in the Atlantic in 1918.

name: Carpet sea squirt
fact: The carpet sea squirt spreads over the seabed in smothering mats and is an invader on coasts around the world.

name: Carpet shark
fact: Carpet sharks are flattened, camouflaged seabed dwellers, an order that includes wobbegongs, nurse sharks and the whale shark.

name: Carpione
fact: The carpione is a rare trout found nowhere in the world except Italy's Lake Garda.

name: Carrack
fact: The carrack was the big, round-hulled ocean ship of the 1400s and 1500s; Columbus's Santa María and Magellan's Victoria were carracks.

name: Carriacou
fact: Carriacou is the largest of the Grenadine islands and is known for its boat-building tradition.

name: Cartagena Convention
aliases: Convention for the Protection and Development of the Marine Environment of the Wider Caribbean Region
fact: The Cartagena Convention of 1983 is the regional treaty for protecting the marine environment of the wider Caribbean.

name: Cartagena
fact: Cartagena in Spain was founded around 227 BC by the Carthaginians as Qart Hadasht and has a long naval history.

name: Carysfort Reef
fact: Carysfort Reef in the Florida Keys is marked by an iron screw-pile lighthouse built in the 1850s.

name: Casablanca
fact: Casablanca is Morocco's biggest city and its main Atlantic port, famous around the world thanks to the 1942 film.

name: Casper octopus
fact: A ghost-white octopus nicknamed Casper was discovered off Hawaii in 2016 at about 4,000 metres, laying its eggs on dead sponge stalks attached to metal nodules.

name: Caspian seal
fact: The Caspian seal lives only in the landlocked Caspian Sea, where it breeds on winter ice in the north.

name: Caspian tern
fact: The Caspian tern, with a heavy red bill, is the largest tern and plunge-dives for fish on coasts and large lakes.

name: Catamaran
fact: A catamaran has two parallel hulls joined by a frame, a design borrowed from the fishing craft of southern India; the name comes from the Tamil for 'tied wood'.

name: Catania
fact: Catania on the east coast of Sicily lies at the foot of Mount Etna and has been rebuilt after eruptions and earthquakes.

name: Catfish
fact: Catfish are whiskered bottom-dwellers; the channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States, and Vietnamese basa fills supermarket freezers worldwide.

name: Catshark
fact: Catsharks are the largest shark family, with well over a hundred small species, and many lay tough egg cases on the seabed.

name: Caulerpa taxifolia
fact: Caulerpa taxifolia, the 'killer alga', escaped from an aquarium into the Mediterranean in the 1980s and smothered thousands of hectares of seabed.

name: Cauliflower coral
fact: Cauliflower coral grows in knobbly clumps and is one of the first corals to settle on new reef, but also one of the first to bleach.

name: Cayman Brac
fact: Cayman Brac is named after its bluff, which rises about 43 metres, as 'brac' is the Gaelic word for bluff.

name: Cayman Islands
fact: The Cayman Islands are made up of Grand Cayman, Little Cayman and Cayman Brac, which rise steeply from very deep water south of Cuba.

name: Cayman Trough
fact: The Cayman Trough is the deepest part of the Caribbean Sea, at about 7,500 metres, and holds the deepest known hydrothermal vents, the Beebe vent field.

name: CCAMLR
aliases: Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
fact: CCAMLR, established in 1982 and based in Hobart, manages the fishing of krill and other marine life in the Southern Ocean.

name: Celebes Sea
fact: The Celebes Sea between Indonesia and the Philippines is a deep basin of more than 6,000 metres, famous for the rich reefs around Sipadan.

name: Celestial pearl danio
fact: The celestial pearl danio, a 2-centimetre fish spangled with pearly spots, was found in Myanmar in 2006 and caused such a craze that it was nearly collected to extinction.

name: Celtic Sea
fact: The Celtic Sea lies south of Ireland and west of Cornwall and was only given its name in 1921.

name: Cenderawasih Bay
fact: Cenderawasih Bay in Indonesian New Guinea is famous for whale sharks that gather beneath fishing platforms to feed on baitfish.

name: Central American spinner dolphin
fact: The Central American spinner dolphin is a coastal form of spinner dolphin found off the Pacific shores of Central America.

name: Ceratium
fact: Ceratium is a dinoflagellate with long horn-like projections, which help it float and deter grazers.

name: Cero
fact: The cero is a Spanish mackerel of the Caribbean with a row of yellow-orange streaks and spots along its sides.

name: Ceto
fact: Ceto was a Greek primordial sea goddess and mother of sea monsters, including the Graeae and, with Phorcys, the Gorgons.

name: Cetus
fact: Cetus was the sea monster sent by Poseidon against Ethiopia, from which Perseus rescued Andromeda; it is also a constellation.

name: Ceuta
fact: Ceuta is a Spanish port city on the North African coast, facing the Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Ceviche
fact: Ceviche is raw fish cured in lime or lemon juice with onion and chilli, and it is a national dish of Peru.

name: Chabahar
fact: Chabahar in south-east Iran is the country's only port directly on the open Indian Ocean.

name: Chaetoceros
fact: Chaetoceros is a large genus of diatoms with long spines that link cells into chains and help them float.

name: Chagos anemonefish
fact: The Chagos anemonefish is a clownfish named for the Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean.

name: Chagos Marine Protected Area
fact: The Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean was declared a no-take marine reserve in 2010 around some of the cleanest coral reefs in the world.

name: Chain catshark
fact: The chain catshark is named for the chain-like pattern of dark lines on its body, which glows green under blue light.

name: Chain moray
fact: The chain moray of the Caribbean, patterned with yellow chain links, can leave the water to hunt crabs on rocks at low tide.

name: Chalk bass
fact: The chalk bass is a tiny Caribbean sea bass, barely 8 centimetres long, that is both male and female at once and takes turns laying eggs with its partner.

name: Challenger Deep
fact: Challenger Deep, the floor of the Mariana Trench, was first reached by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960.

name: Challenger expedition
fact: The Challenger expedition of 1872 to 1876 was the first major scientific survey of the world's oceans, and it sounded the Mariana Trench.

name: Chambered nautilus
fact: The chambered nautilus adds new chambers to its spiral shell as it grows and adjusts the gas inside them to rise and sink.

name: Chambo
fact: Chambo is the name given to a group of tilapia from Lake Malawi, which are among the favourite food fish in Malawi.

name: Channel catfish
fact: The channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States and the official state fish of several southern and midwestern states.

name: Channel Islands
fact: The Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney and Sark lie off Normandy and were the only British soil occupied by Germany in the Second World War.

name: Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary
fact: The Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary off southern California protects kelp forests where cold northern and warm southern currents meet.

name: Channelled wrack
fact: Channelled wrack lives at the very top of the shore, where it can dry out for days between tides and still revive.

name: Charles Vane
fact: Charles Vane was a Bahamas pirate who refused the royal pardon of 1718 and was hanged in Jamaica in 1721.

name: Charles Wyville Thomson
fact: Charles Wyville Thomson was the chief scientist of the Challenger expedition of 1872 to 1876, which laid the foundations of oceanography.

name: Charleston
fact: Charleston's harbour, where the Ashley and Cooper rivers meet the Atlantic, saw the first shots of the American Civil War at Fort Sumter in 1861.

name: Charybdis
fact: Charybdis was a Greek sea monster who swallowed seawater and spat it out three times a day, creating a deadly whirlpool.

name: Chatham Islands
fact: The Chatham Islands east of New Zealand are among the first inhabited places on Earth to see each new day.

name: Chatham Rise
fact: The Chatham Rise is a broad submarine plateau east of New Zealand that supports one of the country's most important fishing grounds, including hoki.

name: Checkered puffer
fact: The checkered puffer is a western Atlantic puffer with a checkered back that lives in mangroves and seagrass.

name: Chemosynthetic bacteria
fact: Chemosynthetic bacteria make food from the hydrogen sulphide in vent water instead of from sunlight, feeding every animal at a hydrothermal vent.

name: Chennai
fact: Chennai, formerly Madras, grew around Fort St George, founded by the British East India Company in 1639.

name: Cherry barb
fact: The cherry barb, a small red fish from Sri Lankan streams, is far more common in aquariums than in the wild.

name: Chesapeake Bay
fact: Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States and is famous for its blue crabs and oysters.

name: Chester Nimitz
fact: Chester Nimitz commanded the United States Pacific Fleet through most of the Second World War and signed Japan's surrender for the United States in 1945.

name: Chevron butterflyfish
fact: The chevron butterflyfish feeds almost entirely on table corals and defends its coral patch from other fish.

name: Chicama
fact: Chicama in northern Peru is often claimed to be the longest left-hand wave in the world, with rides of well over a kilometre.

name: Chicken liver sponge
fact: The chicken liver sponge is a smooth, dark-brown encrusting sponge named for its colour and texture.

name: Chikyu
fact: Chikyu is a Japanese drilling ship with a derrick about 120 metres above the water, built to drill deeper into the sea floor than any ship before it.

name: Chile
fact: Chile is a ribbon of land about 4,300 kilometres long that has a Pacific coast along its entire western side.

name: Chilean blue whale
fact: Chilean blue whales feed in the Gulf of Corcovado and nearby waters of southern Chile, an important feeding area for the species.

name: Chilean dolphin
fact: The Chilean dolphin is a small, shy dolphin of Chile's fjords, channels and estuaries and is found nowhere else.

name: Chilean hake
fact: The Chilean hake is a major commercial fish of the Pacific coasts of Chile and Peru.

name: Chilean jack mackerel
fact: The Chilean jack mackerel supported one of the largest fisheries in the world in the 1990s, with catches of about 5 million tonnes, before the stock crashed.

name: Chili rasbora
fact: The chili rasbora of Borneo's blackwater streams is a brilliant red fish barely 2 centimetres long, one of the smallest aquarium fish.

name: Chilli crab
fact: Chilli crab is a Singaporean dish of mud crab in a sweet and spicy tomato and chilli sauce.

name: Chiloe
fact: Chiloe is a large island off southern Chile, known for its wooden churches and houses built on stilts.

name: Chimaera
fact: Chimaeras, or ghost sharks, are cartilaginous deep-water relatives of sharks with electric-sensing pores on their rabbit-like heads.

name: China
fact: China's eastern coast faces the Pacific through the Yellow, East China and South China seas.

name: Chinese mitten crab
fact: The Chinese mitten crab has furry claws, lives in rivers but breeds in the sea, and has invaded the Thames, the Elbe and San Francisco Bay.

name: Chinese sturgeon
fact: The Chinese sturgeon, which migrates between the sea and the Yangtze, is critically endangered since dams blocked its spawning grounds.

name: Ching Shih
fact: Ching Shih commanded the Red Flag Fleet of thousands of pirates in early nineteenth-century China, and she retired with her fortune after accepting an amnesty in 1810.

name: Chinook salmon
fact: The chinook, or king salmon, is the largest Pacific salmon and some swim about 3,000 kilometres up the Yukon River to spawn.

name: Chinstrap penguin
fact: Chinstrap penguins feed almost entirely on krill, and their numbers have crashed as warming has thinned the krill swarms near the Antarctic Peninsula.

name: Chios
fact: Chios is the only place in the world that produces mastic gum, taken from the resin of a local tree.

name: Chip log
fact: A chip log is a piece of wood thrown overboard on a knotted line to measure a ship's speed, which is the origin of the knot.

name: Chiton
fact: Chitons wear a shell of eight overlapping plates and can roll into a ball like a woodlouse when prised from a rock.

name: Chittagong
fact: Chittagong, now officially Chattogram, is Bangladesh's busiest seaport on the Bay of Bengal.

name: Chocolate chip sea star
fact: The chocolate chip sea star gets its name from the dark, knobbly spines dotted across its back like chocolate chips.

name: Chocolate gourami
fact: The chocolate gourami is a small brown fish of Southeast Asian swamps that gulps air at the surface.

name: Chocolate surgeonfish
fact: Young chocolate surgeonfish mimic dwarf angelfish, while adults are chocolate brown with an orange patch behind the gill.

name: Chokka squid
fact: Chokka squid gather in huge spawning swarms off South Africa's southern coast, where they are hand-jigged for export as calamari.

name: Christmas Island
fact: Christmas Island, an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, is famous for the annual migration of millions of red crabs.

name: Christmas Island red crab
fact: Tens of millions of Christmas Island red crabs march from the forest to the sea each year to breed, closing roads across the island.

name: Christmas tree worm
fact: The Christmas tree worm lives in a tube bored into coral and unfurls two spiral crowns of tentacles that snap back inside in a blink.

name: Christopher Columbus
fact: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 on a voyage that opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

name: Christopher Condent
fact: Christopher Condent raided around the Indian Ocean in about 1718 to 1720 and then took a pardon and settled in France.

name: Anna's chromodoris
fact: Anna's chromodoris is a blue nudibranch with a yellow-edged mantle that grazes on sponges on Indo-Pacific reefs.

name: Kunie's chromodoris
fact: Kunie's chromodoris is a brightly coloured sea slug of Indo-Pacific reefs that grazes on sponges.

name: Willan's chromodoris
fact: Willan's chromodoris is a colourful reef nudibranch of the western Pacific that grazes on sponges.

name: Marine chronometer
fact: The marine chronometer is a very accurate clock that lets navigators find longitude, and John Harrison perfected one in the eighteenth century.

name: Chub
fact: The chub is a big-mouthed European river fish that will eat almost anything, from cherries to small fish.

name: Chub mackerel
fact: The chub mackerel is one of the world's biggest fish catches, taken in huge numbers off Japan, Chile and Peru, and is the saba of Japanese sushi bars.

name: Chuichi Nagumo
fact: Chuichi Nagumo led the Japanese carrier force that struck Pearl Harbor and that lost four carriers at Midway.

name: Chum salmon
fact: Chum salmon have the widest range of any Pacific salmon, from California to Korea, and spawning males develop tiger-like purple stripes.

name: Chupare stingray
fact: The chupare stingray lives in the shallow waters of the Caribbean and nearby western Atlantic.

name: Chuuk
fact: Chuuk, once called Truk, is a Micronesian island group whose lagoon holds dozens of Second World War shipwrecks.

name: Cichlid
fact: Many cichlids, from African lakes to the Amazon, brood their eggs and fry in their mouths or guard them fiercely as a pair.

name: Cigar wrasse
fact: The cigar wrasse is a long, slender Indo-Pacific wrasse that can change colour to match seagrass or sand.

name: Cindy Van Dover
fact: Cindy Van Dover was the first woman to pilot the submersible Alvin, and she studies life at hydrothermal vents.

name: Cinnamon clownfish
fact: The cinnamon clownfish, or fire clownfish, is a dark red-brown anemonefish with one white head bar and a bluish tint, from the western Pacific.

name: Cioppino
fact: Cioppino is a tomato-based fish stew from San Francisco, created by Italian fishermen who settled there.

name: Cisco
fact: The cisco, or lake herring, schools in cold North American lakes and is a whitefish rather than a true herring.

name: CITES
aliases: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species
fact: CITES is a 1973 treaty regulating international trade in endangered species, including sharks, rays, seahorses and corals.

name: Citrus curing
fact: Citrus curing soaks raw fish in lime or lemon juice, and the acid turns the flesh opaque as if it had been cooked.

name: Civitavecchia
fact: Civitavecchia is the main seaport of Rome and one of the busiest cruise ports in the Mediterranean.

name: Cladoselache
fact: Cladoselache is one of the earliest well-known sharks, preserved in Devonian shales around Cleveland, Ohio, about 370 million years old.

name: Clam
fact: Clams pull themselves through sand with a muscular foot and draw in water through a siphon to filter out food.

name: Clam chowder
fact: Clam chowder is a thick soup of clams and potatoes, creamy in New England and tomato-based in the Manhattan version.

name: Clarion angelfish
fact: The clarion angelfish lives only around Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands and Clipperton, where it cleans parasites from giant manta rays.

name: Clark's anemonefish
fact: Clark's anemonefish is the least fussy clownfish, able to live in all ten species of host anemone, and ranges from the Persian Gulf to Japan.

name: Clawed armhook squid
fact: The clawed armhook squid was the first squid seen brooding its eggs, carrying a sac of thousands of eggs in its arms for months in the deep.

name: Cleaner shrimp
fact: Cleaner shrimp wave their white antennae to advertise a cleaning service, and reef fish queue up and open their mouths to have parasites picked off.

name: Cleaner wrasse
fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs a cleaning station where bigger fish queue to have parasites picked from their skin, gills and even mouths.

name: Cleat
fact: A cleat is a fitting to which a rope is tied off on a boat.

name: Clew
fact: The clew is the lower back corner of a sail, where the sheets are attached.

name: Cliff diving
fact: Cliff diving is diving into the sea from high rocks or platforms, and elite competitors dive from over twenty metres.

name: Climbing perch
fact: The climbing perch breathes air and can travel over land between ponds, pulling itself along with its gill covers and fins.

name: Clingfish
fact: The northern clingfish grips wet, slimy rock with a suction disc on its belly strong enough to hold many times its own weight.

name: Clipper ship
fact: Clipper ships were the fast sailing ships of the mid-1800s, built for speed on the tea and wool runs; Cutty Sark is the most famous survivor.

name: Clipperton Island
fact: Clipperton Island is a tiny uninhabited French atoll in the eastern Pacific, more than 1,000 kilometres from Mexico, ringed by a lagoon and overrun by land crabs.

name: Cloak anemone
fact: The cloak anemone wraps around a hermit crab's shell and extends it as the crab grows, saving the crab from having to move house.

name: Cloud 9
fact: Cloud 9 on Siargao in the Philippines is a thick, hollow right-hand reef break served by a famous boardwalk.

name: Cloud sponge
fact: Cloud sponges build glass sponge reefs off the coast of British Columbia.

name: Cloudbreak
fact: Cloudbreak off Tavarua in Fiji is a powerful left-hand reef wave that has hosted the Fiji Pro.

name: Cloudy catshark
fact: The cloudy catshark is a small shark of the north-west Pacific that lays egg cases fitted with long curling tendrils.

name: Clown coris
fact: The clown coris is an Indo-Pacific wrasse; young fish are white-spotted orange, while old males grow a hump on the forehead.

name: Clown killifish
fact: The clown killifish is a 3-centimetre West African fish with a banded body and a rocket-flame tail that spends its life just under the surface.

name: Clown knifefish
fact: The clown knifefish is a spotted, knife-shaped fish of Southeast Asia that rises to gulp air.

name: Clown loach
fact: The clown loach, orange with black bands, clicks audibly, sleeps on its side and can grow to 30 centimetres.

name: Clown nudibranch
fact: The clown nudibranch is a white sea slug with orange-tipped bumps that feeds on bryozoans along the Pacific coast of North America.

name: Clown pleco
fact: The clown pleco is a small, orange-banded armoured catfish from Venezuela that rasps and eats sunken wood.

name: Clown surgeonfish
fact: The clown surgeonfish is striped in blue and yellow and fiercely defends its algae patch with a razor-sharp tail spine.

name: Clown triggerfish
fact: The clown triggerfish has large white spots on its black belly and a yellow mouth, making it one of the most recognisable reef fish.

name: Clownfish
fact: Clownfish are immune to the stings of their host anemone, and if the female of a group dies the largest male changes sex to take her place.

name: Club tunicate
fact: The club tunicate is a club-shaped sea squirt from the north-west Pacific that has invaded coasts and shellfish farms worldwide.

name: Clymene dolphin
fact: The Clymene dolphin of the Atlantic is the only confirmed case of a marine mammal species that arose as a hybrid, from spinner and striped dolphins.

name: Coastal defence ship
fact: A coastal defence ship was a small battleship built mainly to protect a nation's own coasts, and Scandinavian navies built many.

name: Coastal spotted dolphin
fact: The coastal spotted dolphin is a nearshore form of the pantropical spotted dolphin found along the Pacific coast of the Americas.

name: Coasteering
fact: Coasteering is travelling along a rocky coastline by climbing, scrambling, swimming and jumping into the sea, and the sport began in Wales.

name: Coastguard
fact: Coastguards patrol coastal waters and run search and rescue, and they enforce maritime law.

name: Cobb Seamount
fact: Cobb Seamount, about 500 kilometres off Washington State, is a flat-topped underwater volcano whose summit lies just a few dozen metres below the surface.

name: Cobia
fact: Cobia is a fast-growing open-water fish now farmed in sea cages in Vietnam, Taiwan and Panama for its firm white flesh.

name: Coccolithophore
fact: Coccolithophores are single-celled algae armoured with chalk discs, and their blooms can turn whole seas milky white in satellite images.

name: Cockatoo waspfish
fact: The cockatoo waspfish rocks gently like a drifting leaf, and its tall dorsal fin carries venomous spines.

name: Cockle
fact: Cockles live buried just under the sand of tidal flats and can leap away from predators by flexing their foot.

name: Cock's comb oyster
fact: The cock's comb oyster has a zigzag shell edge like a rooster's comb and lives fixed to coral and rock.

name: Cocoa damselfish
fact: The cocoa damselfish is a small Caribbean damselfish that is brown as an adult and brightly coloured when young.

name: Coconut crab
fact: The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod, climbs trees and cracks coconuts with claws whose pinch, estimated at up to about 3,300 newtons, is stronger than most animals' bites.

name: Coconut octopus
fact: The coconut octopus carries coconut shells across the seabed to use as a portable shelter, one of the clearest examples of tool use in an invertebrate.

name: Cocos Island
fact: Cocos Island, about 550 kilometres off Costa Rica, is a World Heritage site where divers come for huge schools of scalloped hammerheads.

name: Cocos Islands
fact: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are two Australian atolls in the Indian Ocean that Charles Darwin visited in 1836 while developing his ideas on atoll formation.

name: Cod
fact: Atlantic cod built the economies of Newfoundland and New England and is the classic fish of British fish and chips; its stocks collapsed off Canada in 1992.

name: Coelacanth
fact: The coelacanth was thought extinct for 66 million years until a fisherman landed one off South Africa in 1938; it lives in caves around 200 metres down.

name: Cog
fact: The cog was the sturdy single-masted cargo ship of the medieval Hanseatic League, trading across the North Sea and the Baltic.

name: Coho salmon
fact: Coho, or silver salmon, spend about a year in fresh water and roughly 18 months at sea before returning to spawn with hooked jaws and red flanks.

name: Cold-seep tubeworm
fact: Tubeworms at cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico grow so slowly that some are estimated to be more than 200 years old, among the longest-lived of all animals.

name: Cold smoking
fact: Cold smoking flavours and preserves fish at low temperatures, below about 30 degrees Celsius, without cooking it, as in smoked salmon.

name: Coleman shrimp
fact: Coleman shrimps live in pairs on the venomous fire urchin, clearing a patch of spines to sit among its brilliant colours.

name: Coleman's pygmy seahorse
fact: Coleman's pygmy seahorse is a tiny seahorse, under 3 centimetres long, found in the western Pacific.

name: Collared carpetshark
fact: The collared carpetshark is a small, slender shark with a dark collar-like band behind its head, found off Australia.

name: Collector urchin
fact: The collector urchin covers itself with shell and seaweed fragments, and is used in Hawaii to help control invasive algae.

name: Colombia
fact: Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.

name: Colombo
fact: Colombo, on Sri Lanka's west coast, lies on the main shipping lane between the Suez Canal and the Strait of Malacca.

name: Colossal squid
fact: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is the heaviest invertebrate on Earth, reaching about 500 kilograms, with swivelling hooks on its tentacles.

name: Columbus crab
fact: The Columbus crab lives on floating sargassum and on the backs of loggerhead turtles, hitching rides across the open Atlantic.

name: Columbus's first voyage
fact: On his first voyage in 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed with the Santa Maria, Nina and Pinta and made landfall in the Bahamas.

name: Comb jelly
fact: Comb jellies are not true jellyfish: they swim with eight rows of beating cilia that scatter light into rainbows, and most species also glow blue in the dark.

name: Commerson's dolphin
fact: Commerson's dolphin, with its black-and-white panda colouring, lives off Patagonia and, oddly, in the far-off Kerguelen Islands.

name: Common brittle star
fact: The common brittle star can form carpets of millions of animals on the seabed, each holding its arms up to trap food.

name: Common clubhook squid
fact: The common clubhook squid has sharp hooks on its tentacle clubs and lives in warm and temperate oceans worldwide.

name: Common cockle
fact: The common cockle burrows in sandy European shores and can leap away from danger by flicking its muscular foot.

name: Common cuttlefish
fact: The common cuttlefish has W-shaped pupils and can send rippling waves of colour across its skin even though it is thought to be colour-blind.

name: Common dolphin
fact: Common dolphins have a bold hourglass pattern on their sides and gather in superpods of thousands.

name: Common eider
fact: The common eider is a sea duck of Arctic and northern coasts whose soft down has long been used to fill quilts.

name: Common guillemot
fact: Common guillemots, called murres in North America, swim down after fish to depths of over 100 metres and lay a single pointed egg on a bare cliff ledge.

name: Common loon
fact: The common loon, or great northern diver, breeds on lakes but winters on the sea, chasing fish underwater with powerful kicks of its feet.

name: Common octopus
fact: The common octopus can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak and is a famous escape artist in aquariums and research labs.

name: Common prawn
fact: The common prawn of European rock pools is almost transparent with faint stripes, and is netted along British and Irish coasts for the table.

name: Common skate
fact: The common skate, once abundant in European seas, can grow over 2 metres long and is now critically endangered.

name: Common starfish
fact: The common starfish of the North Atlantic pries open mussels and pushes its stomach out through its mouth to digest them inside the shell.

name: Common stingray
fact: The common stingray of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean was described by ancient Greek and Roman writers, who feared its venomous spine.

name: Common sunstar
fact: The common sunstar has between about 8 and 14 arms ringed in red and white and preys on other starfish.

name: Common thresher shark
fact: The common thresher's scythe-like upper tail lobe can make up half of its total length.

name: Comoros
fact: The Comoros are a volcanic archipelago in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and the African mainland.

name: Compass
fact: A magnetic compass has a needle that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, and Chinese and European sailors used it to steer for centuries.

name: Compass jellyfish
fact: The compass jellyfish has brown V-shaped markings radiating across its bell like the points of a compass, and it starts life male and becomes female.

name: Conch
fact: The queen conch builds a heavy pink-lipped shell and hops along the seabed by pole-vaulting on a claw-like foot.

name: Cone snail
fact: Cone snails fire a venomous harpoon from their beautiful shells, and a few species can kill a person.

name: Confit
fact: Confit cooks fish slowly in oil at a low temperature, and the result is very tender.

name: Conger eel
fact: Conger eel, anago, is a saltwater eel simmered until soft and served with a sweet sauce in sushi; it is leaner than freshwater unagi.

name: Congo tetra
fact: Male Congo tetras of the Congo basin shimmer with rainbow colours and have long, flowing fins.

name: Conodont
fact: Conodonts were eel-like early vertebrates known mainly from tiny tooth-like fossils, which geologists use to date rocks.

name: Container ship
fact: The biggest container ships are about 400 metres long and can carry more than 20,000 standard shipping containers.

name: Conte di Savoia
fact: The Conte di Savoia was an Italian liner of 1932 fitted with huge gyroscopes to reduce rolling.

name: Convict cichlid
fact: The convict cichlid, striped like a prison uniform, breeds so readily that it is used to study parental care in fish.

name: Convict tang
fact: The convict tang is a pale surgeonfish with black bars like a prisoner's uniform that grazes in huge schools that overwhelm territorial damselfish.

name: Cook's first voyage
fact: On his first voyage of 1768 to 1771 in the Endeavour, James Cook observed the transit of Venus at Tahiti and charted New Zealand and Australia's east coast.

name: Cook Inlet
fact: Cook Inlet in Alaska is named after Captain James Cook, who explored it in 1778.

name: Cook Islands
fact: The Cook Islands are 15 islands in the South Pacific named after Captain James Cook and self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

name: Cook Strait
fact: Cook Strait separates New Zealand's North and South Islands and is named after Captain James Cook, who sailed through it in 1770.

name: Cookiecutter shark
fact: The small cookiecutter shark bites neat round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna and even the rubber domes of submarines.

name: Cooper
fact: A cooper makes the barrels used on ships to carry water, salted meat and other provisions.

name: Copacabana
fact: Copacabana in Rio de Janeiro is a crescent of sand about four kilometres long, famous for its wave-patterned pavement and New Year's Eve crowds.

name: Copepod
fact: Copepods are the most numerous animals in the sea by a wide margin, and have been found in the mud at the bottom of the Challenger Deep.

name: Copper shark
fact: Copper sharks, also called bronze whalers, take their name from the bronze sheen of their skin and follow the winter sardine run off South Africa.

name: Copperband butterflyfish
fact: The copperband butterflyfish has a long snout for picking food from crevices and a false eyespot on its dorsal fin; aquarists use it to eat pest anemones.

name: Coquina
fact: Tiny coquina clams repeatedly dig in and out of the sand as waves wash up the beach.

name: Coracle
fact: A coracle is a small, round boat of woven wood covered in hide or canvas, still used by a few fishermen in Wales and India.

name: Coral
fact: Coral is built by tiny animals called polyps, each a ring of stinging tentacles around a mouth, which together lay down reefs visible from space.

name: Coral beauty
fact: The coral beauty is a hardy dwarf angelfish, purple-blue with an orange belly, that is one of the most commonly kept marine angelfish.

name: Coral bleaching
fact: Coral bleaching happens when warm water stresses corals into expelling the algae that give them colour and food.

name: Coral catshark
fact: The coral catshark hides in reef crevices by day and is small enough that it is often kept in home aquariums.

name: Coral goby
fact: Coral gobies are tiny fish that live their whole lives among the branches of a single Acropora coral colony, which they defend from seaweed.

name: Coral guard crab
fact: Coral guard crabs live among the branches of a coral and defend it against predators such as crown-of-thorns starfish.

name: Coral hind
fact: The coral hind is a vivid orange-red grouper covered in bright blue spots, common on Indo-Pacific and Red Sea reefs.

name: Coral Restoration Foundation
fact: The Coral Restoration Foundation, based in Key Largo, Florida, grows coral in underwater nurseries and plants it back onto damaged reefs.

name: Coral Sea
fact: The Coral Sea off north-east Australia contains the Great Barrier Reef, and a 1942 battle fought there was the first in which opposing ships never sighted each other.

name: Coral Triangle Initiative
fact: The Coral Triangle Initiative of 2009 is a partnership of six countries, including Indonesia and the Philippines, to protect the Coral Triangle's reefs and fisheries.

name: Coral trout
fact: The coral trout is a red, blue-spotted grouper of the Great Barrier Reef, not a trout at all, and one of the most valuable fish in Queensland's reef fishery.

name: Coralline algae
fact: Coralline algae are red seaweeds that lay down hard limestone skeletons, cementing coral reefs together like pink mortar.

name: Cordouan Lighthouse
fact: Cordouan Lighthouse stands on a rock in the Gironde estuary in France, was completed in 1611, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

name: Corfu
fact: Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea whose old town is a World Heritage Site and which was long ruled by Venice.

name: Corinth Canal
fact: The Corinth Canal in Greece, opened in 1893, is about 6.3 kilometres long and cuts through rock walls nearly 80 metres high.

name: Corinto
fact: Corinto is Nicaragua's principal Pacific port.

name: Cork
fact: Cork harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and Cobh at its mouth was the Titanic's last port of call.

name: Corkwing wrasse
fact: The corkwing wrasse of European coasts builds a nest of seaweed in a rock crevice, which the male guards until the eggs hatch.

name: Cormorant
fact: Cormorants have feathers that soak up water, which helps them dive after fish, so they stand with wings spread to dry afterwards.

name: Cornetfish
fact: The cornetfish is an extremely slender reef fish up to 1.5 metres long, with a tubular snout and a whip-like filament trailing from its tail.

name: Corsica
fact: Corsica is a mountainous French island and the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born in Ajaccio in 1769.

name: Cortez round stingray
fact: The Cortez round stingray is a small, round-bodied ray found only in the Gulf of California.

name: Corvette
fact: Corvettes are the smallest class of warship that is still regarded as an ocean-going combatant, and hundreds were built to escort convoys in the Second World War.

name: Corvina
fact: Corvinas are drum fish of the eastern Pacific and elsewhere that croak with swim-bladder muscles, and some gather in deafening spawning choruses.

name: Corydoras
fact: Corydoras catfish dart to the surface to gulp air and absorb the oxygen through the lining of the gut.

name: Costa Concordia
fact: The cruise ship Costa Concordia struck rocks and capsized off the Italian island of Giglio in January 2012; it was refloated two years later and scrapped.

name: Costa Rica
fact: Costa Rica has coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea and protects a large share of its land as national parks.

name: Cotabato Trench
fact: The Cotabato Trench lies off Mindanao in the Philippines and was the source of the 1976 Moro Gulf earthquake and tsunami.

name: Cotton spinner
fact: When threatened, the cotton spinner shoots out sticky white threads that tangle around an attacker.

name: Cousteau Society
fact: The Cousteau Society was founded by Jacques Cousteau in 1973 to protect the oceans and educate the public.

name: Cownose ray
fact: Cownose rays migrate in schools of thousands along the US east coast and feed by digging clams out of the sand.

name: Cowrie
fact: Cowrie shells stay smooth and glossy because the living animal wraps its mantle over the outside, and they once served as money across Africa and Asia.

name: Cowtail stingray
fact: The cowtail stingray has a flap of skin under its tail like a feather, and its rough skin has been used to make shagreen leather.

name: Cox's Bazar
fact: Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh is a natural sea beach about 120 kilometres long and is often called the longest in the world.

name: Coxswain
fact: A coxswain steers a small boat, a role in lifeboats and rowing crews that also includes command of the crew.

name: Cozumel
fact: Cozumel lies off Mexico's Yucatán coast and is known for drift diving along the Mesoamerican Reef.

name: Cozumel Reefs National Park
fact: Cozumel's reefs off Mexico's Yucatán are known for drift diving, where the current carries divers along walls such as Palancar and Santa Rosa.

name: Crab
fact: Crabs must shed their hard shells to grow, hiding away while the soft new shell underneath hardens.

name: Crab boat
fact: Crab boats work the Bering Sea in winter, hauling heavy steel pots in freezing seas, a job made famous by the television series Deadliest Catch.

name: Crab cakes
fact: Crab cakes are patties of crab meat, bound and fried or baked, and they are strongly associated with Maryland.

name: Crab-eating macaque
fact: Crab-eating macaques forage in South-East Asian mangroves at low tide, cracking crabs and shellfish, and some use stone tools to do it.

name: Crab larva
fact: Crab larvae, called zoea, drift in the plankton wearing a spiky helmet and look nothing like the adults they will become.

name: Crab rangoon
fact: Crab rangoon is a deep-fried dumpling filled with cream cheese and crab, found in American Chinese restaurants.

name: Crabeater seal
fact: Crabeater seals do not eat crabs at all; they strain krill through their intricately lobed teeth and are probably the most numerous seal on Earth.

name: Crayfish
