fact: Sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells, and females return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.

name: Sea urchin
fact: A sea urchin's spines sit on a rigid shell called a test, which is made of plates of calcium carbonate.

name: Sea Venture voyage
fact: The Sea Venture was wrecked on Bermuda in 1609 while sailing to Jamestown, and the story may have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest.

name: Sea walnut
fact: The sea walnut, a comb jelly from the American Atlantic, invaded the Black Sea in ballast water and helped collapse its anchovy fishery in the 1980s.

name: Sea wasp
fact: The sea wasp, a box jellyfish of northern Australia, carries enough venom in its tentacles to kill a person within minutes.

name: Sea whip
fact: A sea whip is a soft coral that grows as a single long, flexible rod, often brightly coloured, swaying in the current.

name: Seagrass
fact: Seagrasses are true flowering plants, not seaweeds, with roots and underwater flowers, and their meadows store carbon far faster than forests on land.

name: Seahorse
fact: Seahorses are reef fish that swim upright, grip coral with their tails, and leave the males to carry the eggs in a pouch.

name: Seal
fact: Seals are marine mammals with streamlined bodies and flippers, and true seals have no external ear flaps.

name: Seamoth
fact: Seamoths are small armoured fish with wing-like fins and a long flat snout, and they walk across the sand on their pelvic fins.

name: Seaplane tender
fact: A seaplane tender was a ship that supported seaplanes, carrying and servicing them at sea, and the first aircraft carriers grew from them.

name: SeaQuest DSV
fact: SeaQuest DSV was an American television series that began in 1993, set aboard a futuristic submarine exploring the oceans.

name: Seattle
fact: Seattle on Puget Sound, an inlet of the Pacific, was the main outfitting port for the 1897 Klondike Gold Rush.

name: Seaweed farmer
fact: Seaweed farmers grow kelp and other seaweeds on ropes or nets in coastal waters.

name: Seawise Giant
fact: Seawise Giant, later renamed Knock Nevis, was the longest ship ever built, at about 458 metres from bow to stern.

name: Sebae clownfish
fact: The sebae clownfish is a dark anemonefish with a yellow tail and two white bars from the northern Indian Ocean; many fish sold under its name are actually Clark's.

name: Secchi disk
fact: A Secchi disk is a white disc lowered into the sea until it disappears from sight, which measures how clear the water is.

name: The Secret of the Unicorn
fact: The Secret of the Unicorn is Hergé's 1943 Tintin comic album in which Tintin follows clues to a lost pirate treasure from a model ship.

name: Sediment trap
fact: A sediment trap is a funnel moored in the sea that collects the marine snow falling to the deep.

name: Sedna
fact: Sedna is the Inuit goddess of the sea and its animals, and in many tellings the seals and whales were created from her severed fingers.

name: Seehund
fact: The Seehund was a German two-man midget submarine of the Second World War, built in large numbers in 1944 and 1945.

name: Seep tubeworm
fact: Seep tubeworms living around cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico have been aged at over 250 years, making them among the longest-lived animals known.

name: Segonzacia mesatlantica
fact: Segonzacia mesatlantica is a crab that lives around hot vents on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

name: Sei whale
fact: The sei whale is one of the fastest great whales and was hunted hard in the 1960s once fin whale numbers had collapsed.

name: Seiche
fact: A seiche is a standing wave that sloshes back and forth in an enclosed or semi-enclosed body of water, such as a bay or lake.

name: Selkie
fact: Selkies are seals in Scottish and Irish folklore that can shed their skins to take human form on land.

name: Senegal
fact: Senegal's capital, Dakar, sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa, on the Atlantic.

name: Senegal bichir
fact: The Senegal bichir has paired lungs and is sometimes sold in aquariums as the dinosaur eel for its ancient look.

name: Senegalese sole
fact: The Senegalese sole lives in the eastern Atlantic from the Bay of Biscay to West Africa and is farmed in southern Europe.

name: Señorita
fact: The señorita is a slim, cigar-shaped wrasse of California's kelp forests that cleans parasites off other fish and sleeps buried in sand.

name: Sentry
fact: Sentry is an autonomous underwater vehicle from Woods Hole that surveys the deep seafloor without a cable to the ship.

name: Sergeant major
fact: The sergeant major is a striped damselfish found on reefs around the world, named for the stripes on a sergeant's sleeve; it swarms around divers for crumbs.

name: Sergey Gorshkov
fact: Sergey Gorshkov led the Soviet Navy from 1956 to 1985 and turned it into a global ocean-going force.

name: Serra Spanish mackerel
fact: The serra Spanish mackerel is a fast-swimming mackerel of the western Atlantic, from the Caribbean down to Brazil.

name: Serrated ribbon seagrass
fact: Serrated ribbon seagrass has finely toothed leaf tips and grows in shallow waters across the Indo-West Pacific.

name: Serrated wrack
fact: Serrated wrack is the toothed-edged brown seaweed of the lower shore, with no air bladders, sheltering many small animals beneath it.

name: Serving raw
fact: Serving fish raw, as in sashimi, poke or tartare, depends on fish that is very fresh or has been frozen first.

name: Seto Inland Sea
fact: The Seto Inland Sea separates three of Japan's main islands, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, and is dotted with about 3,000 islands.

name: Setubal
fact: Setubal is a Portuguese port on the Sado estuary, known for its resident bottlenose dolphins.

name: Sevan trout
fact: The Sevan trout is found naturally only in Lake Sevan in Armenia and is endangered after the lake was lowered for irrigation and power.

name: Seven-arm octopus
fact: The seven-arm octopus is one of the largest octopuses, with a 4-metre specimen known, and has been photographed holding and eating jellyfish.

name: Seven-armed starfish
fact: The seven-armed starfish has seven arms rather than five and hunts other starfish and brittle stars in the north-east Atlantic.

name: Seven-figure pygmy goby
fact: The seven-figure pygmy goby, a 2-centimetre reef fish, has the shortest lifespan of any vertebrate, living for about two months.

name: Seven Mile Beach
fact: Despite its name, Seven Mile Beach on Grand Cayman is only about five and a half miles long.

name: Sevengill shark
fact: Sevengill sharks have seven pairs of gill slits where most sharks have five.

name: Sevenstar flying squid
fact: The sevenstar flying squid is a Southern Ocean squid that is an important food for albatrosses and seals.

name: Severn's pygmy seahorse
fact: Severn's pygmy seahorse is a tiny pygmy seahorse only about 2.5 centimetres long.

name: Sewol
fact: The South Korean ferry Sewol capsized and sank in April 2014 with the loss of more than 300 people, most of them schoolchildren.

name: Sextant
fact: A sextant measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon, letting a navigator work out latitude.

name: Sexy shrimp
fact: The sexy shrimp got its name from the way it constantly sways its tail up and down while sitting on a sea anemone.

name: Seychelles
fact: The Seychelles are an archipelago of about 115 islands in the western Indian Ocean.

name: Seychelles anemonefish
fact: The Seychelles anemonefish is found only around the Seychelles, Mauritius and nearby Indian Ocean islands.

name: Sfax
fact: Sfax is Tunisia's second-largest city and a major Mediterranean port.

name: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
fact: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium in Pudong opened in 2002 and is known for a long acrylic tunnel through its tanks.

name: Shanny
fact: The shanny is a common rock pool fish that can survive out of water for hours by sheltering damp under seaweed.

name: Shark
fact: Every shark has ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores on its snout that detect the faint electric fields of a hidden animal's muscles and heartbeat.

name: Shark Bay seagrass
fact: The Posidonia australis meadow in Shark Bay, Western Australia, is the largest known plant in the world, covering about 180 square kilometres and some 4,500 years old.

name: Shark Trust
fact: The Shark Trust is a British charity founded in 1997 that works for the conservation of sharks and rays.

name: Sharpnose puffer
fact: The sharpnose puffer is a thumb-sized Caribbean puffer with a pointed snout and bright blue lines around its eyes.

name: Sharpnose sevengill shark
fact: The sharpnose sevengill is a slender deep-water shark with seven gill slits and large green eyes.

name: Sharptail mola
fact: The sharptail mola is a relative of the ocean sunfish that has a pointed tail lobe and wanders the open ocean.

name: Shastasaurus
fact: Shastasaurus was a large, slender-snouted ichthyosaur of the Late Triassic, named after Shasta County in California.

name: Shearwater
fact: Shearwaters skim the waves on stiff wings and dive after fish and squid, some chasing them tens of metres down.

name: Shedd Aquarium
fact: Chicago's Shedd Aquarium opened in 1930 and was the first inland aquarium with a permanent saltwater collection.

name: Sheepshead
fact: The sheepshead of the Gulf of Mexico has eerily human-looking teeth for crunching barnacles and crabs off pilings.

name: Shell Beach
fact: Shell Beach in Shark Bay, Western Australia, is made almost entirely of tiny cockle shells and runs for about 60 kilometres.

name: Shell-dwelling cichlid
fact: This tiny cichlid of Lake Tanganyika lives in empty snail shells on the lake bed and defends a territory of shells like a miniature colony.

name: Shepherd's beaked whale
fact: Shepherd's beaked whale is the only beaked whale with a full set of functional teeth in both jaws.

name: Shetland
fact: Shetland is the northernmost part of the British Isles, closer to Norway than to Edinburgh, with a long Norse history.

name: Shingle urchin
fact: The shingle urchin has flat, blunt spines that fit together like roof tiles, helping it hold on in pounding surf.

name: Shinkai 2000
fact: Shinkai 2000 was a Japanese crewed research submersible that could dive to 2,000 metres.

name: Shinkai 6500
fact: Japan's Shinkai 6500 can dive to 6,500 metres and was for many years the deepest-diving crewed research submersible in service.

name: Shinkaia crosnieri
fact: Shinkaia crosnieri is a squat lobster of Okinawa Trough vents that carries chemosynthetic bacteria on its bristles.

name: Ship's captain
fact: A ship's captain, also called the master, is the officer with ultimate command and legal responsibility for a vessel.

name: Ship's carpenter
fact: The ship's carpenter was responsible for the hull and masts, plugging leaks and mending damage in the age of sail.

name: Ship chandler
fact: A ship chandler supplies provisions and equipment, such as rope, paint and lamps, to ships in port.

name: Ship's cook
fact: The ship's cook prepares the crew's meals in the galley and is vital to morale on a long voyage.

name: Ship of the line
fact: Ships of the line were the biggest sailing warships, built to fight in a single line with rows of cannon along their sides.

name: Ship's surgeon
fact: A ship's surgeon looked after the health of a ship's crew, and in naval history he was often also the ship's naturalist.

name: Shipbreaker
fact: Shipbreakers take apart old ships to recycle the steel, much of it done on beaches in South Asia.

name: Shipworm
fact: Shipworms are bivalves with long, worm-like bodies that bore through wood and once threatened wooden ships.

name: Shipwright
fact: A shipwright builds and repairs wooden ships and boats.

name: Shoal grass
fact: Shoal grass is a thin-bladed seagrass of the western Atlantic that is often the first to colonise shallow, disturbed sand.

name: Shonisaurus
fact: Shonisaurus was a Triassic ichthyosaur the size of a bus, and dozens of its skeletons lie together at Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park in Nevada.

name: Shore crab
fact: The shore crab, the common rock-pool crab of Europe, has spread around the world in ships' ballast water and is one of the most invasive marine species.

name: Shore rockling
fact: The shore rockling is a small, eel-like cod relative with three barbels, found under stones in rock pools around Britain.

name: Short-beaked common dolphin
fact: Short-beaked common dolphins carry an hourglass pattern of grey, yellow and white on their sides and often gather in very large, fast-moving pods.

name: Short-beaked echidna
fact: The short-beaked echidna has electroreceptors in its snout that detect the weak electrical signals of its insect prey.

name: Short-finned eel
fact: The short-finned eel of Australia and New Zealand migrates thousands of kilometres to spawn in the Coral Sea.

name: Short-finned pilot whale
fact: Short-finned pilot whales sprint after squid in the deep, earning the nickname 'cheetahs of the deep', and females live decades past menopause.

name: Short mackerel
fact: The short mackerel is a plankton-feeding mackerel of the Indo-West Pacific, heavily fished and eaten in Thailand.

name: Short-nosed sea snake
fact: The short-nosed sea snake was feared extinct for 15 years until a pair was photographed courting on Ningaloo Reef in 2015.

name: Short-snouted seahorse
fact: The short-snouted seahorse is one of two seahorse species native to British waters and has even been found in the Thames estuary.

name: Short-tail stingray
fact: The short-tail stingray is among the largest stingrays, reaching over 2 metres across and about 350 kilograms.

name: Short-tailed albatross
fact: The short-tailed albatross was feared extinct in the 1940s before a few breeding birds were found on a Japanese island.

name: Short-tailed shearwater
fact: Short-tailed shearwaters, Australia's muttonbirds, loop around the Pacific to Alaska and back each year, a journey of roughly 30,000 kilometres.

name: Shortbill spearfish
fact: The shortbill spearfish is a slim, fast billfish of the Pacific with a bill barely longer than its lower jaw.

name: Shortfin mako
fact: Shortfin makos keep their bodies warmer than the surrounding water, which powers their famous bursts of speed.

name: Shortnose gar
fact: The shortnose gar lives in the Mississippi basin and gulps air at the surface to survive in warm, stagnant water.

name: Shortraker rockfish
fact: The shortraker rockfish of the North Pacific has been aged at more than 150 years, making it one of the longest-lived fish.

name: Shortspine spurdog
fact: The shortspine spurdog is a small dogfish with a spine in front of each dorsal fin, living on deep slopes and seamounts in many seas.

name: Shortspine thornyhead
fact: The shortspine thornyhead lives deep on the North Pacific slope and can live to over 100 years.

name: Shovelnose guitarfish
fact: The shovelnose guitarfish is a ray with a pointed shovel-shaped snout and a shark-like tail, lying on sandy bottoms off California and Mexico.

name: Shovelnose sorubim
fact: The shovelnose sorubim is a South American catfish with a long, flat, spade-shaped snout.

name: Shrimp
fact: Shrimps and prawns wear a thin, flexible shell that they shed many times as they grow.

name: Shrimp goby
fact: Shrimp gobies stand guard at the mouth of a burrow dug by a pistol shrimp, warning the shrimp with a flick of the tail when danger approaches.

name: Shrimp scampi
fact: Shrimp scampi is shrimp cooked in garlic, butter and white wine, and the dish is an Italian-American adaptation named for langoustines.

name: Shrimpfish
fact: Shrimpfish, or razorfish, are thin armoured relatives of seahorses that swim head-down in synchronised groups, often hiding among sea urchin spines.

name: Siamese algae eater
fact: The Siamese algae eater is valued by aquarists because it is one of the few fish that eats stringy black beard algae.

name: Siberut
fact: Siberut is the largest of the Mentawai Islands off Sumatra and is home to several primates found nowhere else.

name: Sicily
fact: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and is home to Mount Etna, one of the most active volcanoes in the world.

name: Sicklefin lemon shark
fact: The sicklefin lemon shark is the Indo-Pacific cousin of the lemon shark and is a favourite of shark-feeding dives in French Polynesia.

name: Side-scan sonar
fact: Side-scan sonar is towed behind a ship and sends sound sideways to build images of the seabed, and it is often used to find wrecks.

name: Sierra Leone
fact: Sierra Leone's capital, Freetown, stands on a large natural harbour on the Atlantic coast.

name: Signal crayfish
fact: The signal crayfish, named for the white patch at its claw joints, was introduced from North America and now dominates rivers across Europe.

name: Silfra
fact: Silfra in Iceland is a flooded crack between the North American and Eurasian plates, with glacial water so clear that visibility exceeds 100 metres.

name: Silhouette Island
fact: Silhouette Island is a mountainous island in the Seychelles, most of which is a national park.

name: Silky shark
fact: Silky sharks get their name from the smooth feel of their skin and are among the most heavily fished sharks in the world.

name: Silver carp
fact: The silver carp is among the most farmed fish in the world in China, yet in American rivers it is an invader notorious for leaping out of the water at boats.

name: Silver-cheeked toadfish
fact: The silver-cheeked toadfish, a highly toxic puffer, spread from the Red Sea through the Suez Canal and now plagues fisheries across the Mediterranean.

name: Silver dollar
fact: The silver dollar is a flat, coin-shaped Amazon fish kept in aquariums, a plant-eating cousin of the piranha.

name: Silver hake
fact: The silver hake is the main hake of the US east coast, a fast-swimming predator of small fish that is sold there under the name whiting.

name: Silver perch
fact: The silver perch is a small drum of US Atlantic estuaries that joins loud evening drumming choruses in summer, picked up by hydrophones in Chesapeake Bay.

name: Silvertip shark
fact: Silvertip sharks, with white edges on every fin, patrol the drop-offs of Indo-Pacific reefs and are bold around divers.

name: Simeulue
fact: Simeulue is an Indonesian island off Sumatra where the local oral tradition of fleeing to high ground after an earthquake saved many lives in the 2004 tsunami.

name: Sinarapan
fact: The sinarapan of the Philippines is one of the smallest fish known, reaching only about 1.2 centimetres in length.

name: Singapore
fact: Singapore is an island city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula beside the Strait of Malacca.

name: Singapore Strait
fact: The Singapore Strait is a narrow waterway south of Singapore that links the Strait of Malacca with the South China Sea.

name: Sint Eustatius
fact: Sint Eustatius, known as Statia, was a busy trading port in the eighteenth century and is dominated by the Quill volcano.

name: Sipadan
fact: Sipadan, off Malaysian Borneo, is an oceanic island rising 600 metres from the seabed, famed for green turtles and swirling barracuda tornadoes.

name: Siphonophore
fact: A siphonophore is a chain of specialised clones acting as one animal; one filmed off Western Australia in 2020 was estimated at about 45 metres long.

name: Sirens
fact: The Sirens of Greek myth lured sailors onto rocks with their enchanting singing, and Odysseus had himself tied to his mast to hear them safely.

name: Six-line wrasse
fact: The six-line wrasse is a tiny purple-and-orange striped wrasse from Indo-Pacific reefs that hunts pests such as flatworms in aquariums.

name: Sixbar angelfish
fact: The sixbar angelfish is a large Indo-Pacific reef fish whose pale body is crossed by dark vertical bars.

name: Sixgill shark
fact: The bluntnose sixgill shark has six gill slits instead of five, grows to about 5 metres and spends the day down to about 2,500 metres.

name: Sixgill stingray
fact: The sixgill stingray lives in deep water and is the only stingray with six pairs of gill slits instead of five.

name: Skagerrak
fact: The Skagerrak is the strait between Norway, Denmark and Sweden that links the North Sea to the Baltic, and it was the scene of the Battle of Jutland in 1916.

name: Skate
fact: Skates lay their eggs in leathery cases called mermaid's purses that often wash up on beaches.

name: Skeleton Bay
fact: Skeleton Bay in Namibia, near Walvis Bay, is known for extremely long, fast left-hand barrels over sand.

name: Skellig Michael
fact: Skellig Michael is a jagged rock off Ireland with a sixth-century monastery on its summit, later used as Luke Skywalker's hideout in Star Wars.

name: Skerryvore Lighthouse
fact: Skerryvore Lighthouse, built by Alan Stevenson and first lit in 1844, is the tallest lighthouse in Scotland at about 48 metres.

name: Skimboarding
fact: Skimboarding is riding a thin board that is thrown onto the thin sheet of water at the shoreline, then sliding on to catch a wave.

name: Skipjack tuna
fact: Skipjack is the most-caught tuna in the world and the one in most tins; in Japan it is katsuo, dried into bonito flakes and seared as tataki.

name: Sky emperor
fact: The sky emperor is an emperor of the western Indian Ocean that lives around reefs and is fished for food.

name: Slate pencil urchin
fact: The slate pencil urchin's thick, blunt reddish spines look like old-fashioned slate pencils and have been used to make wind chimes and jewellery.

name: Sleeper shark
fact: Sleeper sharks are sluggish cold-water sharks of the deep, and the flesh of some species is toxic until it is fermented or dried.

name: Slender giant moray
fact: The slender giant moray is the longest eel in the world, reaching about 4 metres, and lives in muddy estuaries of the Indo-Pacific.

name: Slender seahorse
fact: The slender seahorse of the Caribbean and Brazil is a popular aquarium species that comes in yellow, orange, red and black.

name: Slender tuna
fact: The slender tuna is a Southern Ocean member of the tuna family that feeds on krill and is rarely seen by anyone but longline crews.

name: Slingjaw wrasse
fact: The slingjaw wrasse can shoot its jaws forward to half its body length to snatch prey, the most extreme jaw protrusion of any fish.

name: Slipper limpet
fact: Slipper limpets live in stacks, with the males on top turning female as they age, and they have become invasive on European coasts.

name: Slipper lobster
fact: Slipper lobsters have flat, plate-like antennae instead of long feelers and are sold in Australia as Moreton Bay bugs and Balmain bugs.

name: Slippery dick
fact: The slippery dick is a common Caribbean wrasse named for its slimy, hard-to-hold body; it changes from a striped female to a greener male.

name: Slit shell snail
fact: Slit shell snails of deep tropical slopes belong to a family with a fossil record back to the Cambrian, around 500 million years ago, and their shells are prized by collectors.

name: Sliteye shark
fact: The sliteye shark is a slim requiem shark of Indo-Pacific shallows with large, slit-like eyes.

name: Joshua Slocum's solo circumnavigation
fact: Joshua Slocum sailed alone around the world in his sloop Spray from 1895 to 1898, the first person to do so.

name: Sloop
fact: A sloop is a sailing boat with a single mast and one headsail, the most common rig on modern yachts.

name: Sloop-of-war
fact: A sloop-of-war was a small sailing warship with guns on one deck, and it was used for patrol and escort duty.

name: Small-headed sea snake
fact: The small-headed sea snake has a tiny head on a slim neck and lives in the shallow waters off northern Australia.

name: Small-spotted catshark
fact: The small-spotted catshark lays its eggs in curly-tendrilled cases known as mermaid's purses and is one of the commonest sharks around Britain.

name: Smalleye pygmy shark
fact: The smalleye pygmy shark is one of the smallest sharks alive, a deep-water species of the Indo-Pacific that stays under 25 centimetres long.

name: Smalleye stingray
fact: The smalleye stingray is a large Indo-West Pacific ray with tiny eyes that lives on soft seabeds.

name: Smallmouth bass
fact: The smallmouth bass prefers cooler, rockier rivers and lakes than its largemouth cousin and fights hard for its size.

name: Smalltooth sand tiger
fact: The smalltooth sand tiger is a bulky deep-water shark that lives down to around 900 metres and is rarely seen alive.

name: Smalltooth sawfish
fact: The smalltooth sawfish was once found from New York to Brazil but now survives mainly in south-west Florida, where it is protected.

name: Smeaton's Tower
fact: Smeaton's Tower on Plymouth Hoe is the upper part of the third Eddystone Lighthouse, moved there stone by stone after 1882.

name: Smelt
fact: European smelt give off a smell like cucumber, which is how many anglers recognise them.

name: Smoking
fact: Smoking preserves and flavours fish with wood smoke, as in smoked salmon, kippers and smoked haddock.

name: Smooth dogfish
fact: The smooth dogfish is a small shark of the western Atlantic that crushes crabs and lobsters with flat, pavement-like teeth.

name: Smooth flower coral
fact: The smooth flower coral forms bushy colonies of large, fleshy flower-like polyps on Caribbean reefs.

name: Smooth hammerhead
fact: The smooth hammerhead has no notch in the middle of its head and ranges further into cool water than other hammerheads.

name: Smooth handfish
fact: The smooth handfish of Tasmania, known from one specimen collected in 1802, was declared extinct in 2020, the first modern marine fish so listed, though the IUCN later reset it to data deficient.

name: Smooth-hound
fact: Smooth-hounds are small, harmless sharks with flat crushing teeth for eating crabs, and anglers catch them along European shores.

name: Smooth ribbon seagrass
fact: Smooth ribbon seagrass grows in shallow tropical waters of the Indo-West Pacific, often on reef flats.

name: Smooth trunkfish
fact: The smooth trunkfish of the Caribbean blows jets of water into the sand to uncover the worms and crustaceans it eats.

name: Smoothback river stingray
fact: The smoothback river stingray is a freshwater ray found in rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins.

name: Snaggletooth shark
fact: The snaggletooth shark has long, hooked, serrated teeth that protrude from its mouth even when it is closed.

name: Snailfish
fact: Snailfish are the deepest-living fish known: one was filmed at 8,336 metres in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench in 2022.

name: Snake eel
fact: Snake eels have a hard, pointed tail that they use to burrow backwards into sand, leaving only the head poking out.

name: Snake mackerel
fact: The snake mackerel is a long, slim, fanged predator of the open tropical ocean that rises toward the surface at night.

name: Snake pipefish
fact: The snake pipefish of the north-east Atlantic has almost no tail fin, and its numbers exploded across the North Sea in the mid-2000s.

name: Snakehead
fact: Snakeheads breathe air with a chamber above their gills and can wriggle short distances over land between ponds.

name: Snakelocks anemone
fact: The snakelocks anemone cannot fully pull in its long green tentacles, which get their colour from algae living inside them and their purple tips from a pigment.

name: Snakeskin gourami
fact: The snakeskin gourami, named for its scaly patterning, breathes air with a labyrinth organ and is widely eaten in Southeast Asia.

name: Snapper
fact: Snappers are schooling reef predators prized as food fish, and the red snapper can live for more than 50 years.

name: Snapper Rocks
fact: Snapper Rocks on Australia's Gold Coast sits at the head of the Superbank, a sand-bottom point break that can run for several hundred metres.

name: Sneaker wave
fact: A sneaker wave is a surprisingly large wave that comes much farther up a beach than the ones before it and can sweep people off their feet.

name: Snipe eel
fact: The snipe eel has a body like a ribbon and thin, outward-curving jaws like a bird's beak that cannot close, which it uses to snag shrimp by their antennae.

name: Snipefish
fact: The snipefish is a small deep-water relative of seahorses with a long tube snout, named after the wading bird with a long bill.

name: Snook
fact: The common snook lives in the mangrove estuaries of Florida and the Gulf of Mexico and changes from male to female as it grows.

name: Snorkelling
fact: Snorkelling is swimming at the surface with a mask and a breathing tube to watch marine life below.

name: Snow crab
fact: Snow crabs live on cold northern seabeds, and billions vanished from the Bering Sea after a marine heatwave, closing the fishery in 2022.

name: Snow petrel
fact: The snow petrel is pure white, breeds farther south than almost any other bird, and has been seen at the South Pole itself.

name: Snowflake moray
fact: The snowflake moray has blunt, pebble-like teeth for crushing crabs and shrimp, and is a popular aquarium moray.

name: Snowy grouper
fact: The snowy grouper lives on deep rocky bottoms of the western Atlantic; its juveniles are dotted with white spots like snow.

name: Snowy sheathbill
fact: The snowy sheathbill is a white scavenger with unwebbed feet that steals eggs and food around Antarctic penguin colonies.

name: Snubnose parasitic eel
fact: The snubnose parasitic eel has been found burrowing into the flesh of other deep-sea fish, though it also scavenges.

name: Sockeye salmon
fact: Sockeye salmon turn brilliant red with green heads when they return from the sea to spawn, and landlocked populations are known as kokanee.

name: Socotra
fact: Socotra lies off the Horn of Africa and more than a third of its plant species grow nowhere else, including the dragon's blood tree.

name: Soft coral
fact: Soft corals have no hard skeleton and sway in the current, supported by tiny limestone needles in their flesh.

name: Soft-shell clam
fact: Soft-shell clams, the 'steamers' of New England clam shacks, have a long neck that squirts water when you walk over the mud flat.

name: Sohal surgeonfish
fact: The sohal tang of the Red Sea is a striped surgeonfish with bright orange tail blades that it uses fiercely to defend its territory against divers and other fish.

name: Soldierfish
fact: Soldierfish are red night-active reef fish that grunt, growl and click with swim-bladder muscles to defend their caves.

name: Sole
fact: Soles are oval, right-eyed flatfish named after the Latin word for a sandal, which the Romans thought they resembled.

name: Solenette
fact: The solenette is a tiny sole, rarely more than 12 centimetres long, that lies on sandy seabeds around Britain and is thrown back by trawlers.

name: Solent
fact: The Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England, famed for yachting and its unusual double high tides.

name: Solomon Islands
fact: The Solomon Islands in the south-west Pacific include Guadalcanal, where a brutal six-month battle was fought in 1942 and 1943.

name: Solomon Sea
fact: The Solomon Sea lies between the Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea and was the scene of fierce naval battles in the Second World War.

name: Somali Current
fact: The Somali Current off the Horn of Africa is one of the few currents that reverses direction, flowing north in the summer monsoon and south in winter.

name: Somalia
fact: Somalia has the longest coastline of mainland Africa, about 3,000 kilometres along the Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden.

name: Somov Sea
fact: The Somov Sea off Antarctica is named after the Soviet oceanographer Mikhail Somov, who led the first Soviet Antarctic expedition.

name: Sonar
fact: Sonar uses sound pulses and their echoes to detect objects and map the seabed underwater.

name: Sooty gull
fact: The sooty gull is a dark brown-grey gull of the Red Sea and Arabian coasts, where it nests on islands and eats fish.

name: Sooty shearwater
fact: Sooty shearwaters fly a figure-of-eight loop around the entire Pacific each year, a round trip of about 64,000 kilometres.

name: Sooty tern
fact: Sooty terns can spend years at sea after fledging, rarely landing on the water, before returning to breed.

name: Sous vide
fact: Sous vide cooks fish sealed in a bag in a water bath at a precisely controlled, low temperature.

name: Sousse
fact: Sousse in Tunisia has a medina that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

name: South Africa
fact: South Africa has both an Atlantic coast, on the west, and an Indian Ocean coast, on the east, and the two oceans meet near Cape Agulhas.

name: South American fur seal
fact: The South American fur seal breeds along the coasts of Peru, Chile, Argentina and Uruguay and the Falkland Islands.

name: South American lungfish
fact: The South American lungfish breathes mostly with its two lungs and digs a burrow in the mud when its swamp dries out.

name: South American sea lion
fact: South American sea lion males have a huge mane-like neck that earned the species its 'lion' name, and some hunt penguins and fur seal pups.

name: South China Sea
fact: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the western Pacific crossed by roughly a third of the world's shipping.

name: South Equatorial Current
fact: The South Equatorial Current flows westward along the equator, and in the Atlantic it splits on the coast of Brazil to feed both the Brazil Current and the Guiana Current.

name: South Georgia
fact: South Georgia is a mountainous, glacier-covered island in the South Atlantic where Ernest Shackleton is buried and millions of king penguins and fur seals breed.

name: South Korea
fact: South Korea has coasts on the Yellow Sea, the Korea Strait and the East Sea, which are all part of the Pacific.

name: South polar skua
fact: The south polar skua breeds on the Antarctic coast, steals penguin eggs and chicks, and has been recorded at the South Pole.

name: South Sandwich Trench
fact: The South Sandwich Trench east of the South Sandwich Islands is the deepest trench in the South Atlantic, reaching about 8,300 metres at the Meteor Deep.

name: South Shetland Trench
fact: The South Shetland Trench north of the Antarctic Peninsula is one of the few ocean trenches in Antarctic waters.

name: Southern blue-ringed octopus
fact: The southern blue-ringed octopus lives in tide pools and shallow reefs of southern Australia and delivers its venom through a bite that is often painless.

name: Southern blue whiting
fact: The southern blue whiting is a cod relative of sub-Antarctic waters fished off New Zealand, Argentina and the Falklands.

name: Southern bluefin tuna
fact: The southern bluefin tuna was fished down to a small fraction of its original numbers and is now ranched in sea pens off South Australia.

name: Southern bottlenose whale
fact: The southern bottlenose whale feeds near the Antarctic ice edge and is one of the most often sighted beaked whales in the Southern Ocean.

name: Southern bull kelp
fact: Southern bull kelp has a honeycomb-like inner flesh that keeps it afloat, and Māori once used its blades as bags to store food.

name: Southern calamari
fact: The southern calamari is a large, fast-growing squid of southern Australian and New Zealand waters that is caught for food.

name: Southern elephant seal
fact: The southern elephant seal is the largest seal and the largest carnivoran, with bulls weighing up to about 4 tonnes.

name: Southern flounder
fact: The southern flounder of the Gulf of Mexico is speared at night by 'floundering' anglers wading the shallows with lights.

name: Southern four-toothed whale
fact: The southern four-toothed whale is a large beaked whale of cold southern seas, named for the two pairs of teeth at the tip of its lower jaw.

name: Southern king crab
fact: The southern king crab lives in the cold waters around Tierra del Fuego and is fished for its large, meaty claws and legs.

name: Southern kingfish
fact: The southern kingfish is a bottom-feeding member of the drum family found along the western Atlantic coast.

name: Southern lanternshark
fact: The southern lanternshark lives on the deep continental slopes of the Southern Hemisphere and carries light-producing organs on its belly.

name: Southern right whale
fact: Southern right whales 'sail' by holding their tail flukes up in the wind, and they gather to calve off Argentina, South Africa and Australia.

name: Southern right whale dolphin
fact: The southern right whale dolphin has no dorsal fin at all and is strikingly black and white.

name: Southern rock lobster
fact: The southern rock lobster is a spiny lobster of southern Australia and New Zealand that shelters in rocky reefs.

name: Southern sand octopus
fact: The southern sand octopus lives on sandy seabeds of southern Australia.

name: Southern sleeper shark
fact: The southern sleeper shark is a large, slow-moving shark of cold southern waters that has been recorded at depths of more than a kilometre.

name: Southern stingray
fact: Southern stingrays gather in the shallows of Stingray City in the Cayman Islands, where they have been hand-fed by visitors for decades.

name: Southland Current
fact: The Southland Current carries subtropical water north-east along the southern and eastern coast of New Zealand's South Island.

name: Sowerby's beaked whale
fact: Sowerby's beaked whale was the first beaked whale described, from an animal stranded in the Moray Firth in Scotland in 1800.

name: Spade-toothed whale
fact: The spade-toothed whale is the rarest whale known; only a handful of specimens have ever been found, and none has been seen alive at sea.

name: Spadenose shark
fact: The spadenose shark is a small shark of Indo-Pacific coasts, caught in large numbers by local fisheries.

name: Spaghetti eel
fact: Spaghetti eels are extremely thin, worm-like eels of the Indo-Pacific that burrow in sand and are found in rivers as well as the sea.

name: Spain
fact: Spain has Atlantic coastlines in Galicia and around Cádiz as well as a long Mediterranean coast.

name: Spangled emperor
fact: The spangled emperor is a widespread Indo-Pacific reef fish and a popular catch for anglers.

name: Spanish Armada
fact: The Spanish Armada of 1588 was scattered by English fireships, gunnery at Gravelines and storms as it tried to invade England.

name: Spanish dancer
fact: The Spanish dancer is a large red nudibranch that swims by flapping its body like a flamenco skirt and lays a red rose-shaped ribbon of eggs.

name: Spanish hogfish
fact: The Spanish hogfish is a purple-and-yellow Caribbean wrasse whose juveniles work as cleaners on larger fish.

name: Spanish ling
fact: The Spanish ling is a deep-water relative of the ling found in the north-east Atlantic and the Mediterranean.

name: Spanish mackerel
fact: The Atlantic Spanish mackerel is a spotted, fast-swimming schooling fish of the US east coast and Gulf of Mexico, popular with anglers and on the plate.

name: Spanish shawl
fact: The Spanish shawl is a purple nudibranch of the California coast with orange frills, which it waves while swimming to escape predators.

name: Spanner crab
fact: The spanner crab walks forwards instead of sideways and has flattened claws shaped like spanners, used to dig into sand.

name: Sparkling gourami
fact: The sparkling gourami is a 4-centimetre fish from Southeast Asia that makes audible croaking sounds when courting or fighting.

name: Sparsely-spotted stingaree
fact: The sparsely-spotted stingaree is a small round-bodied ray of southern Australian waters that lives on sandy seabeds.

name: Spearfishing
fact: Spearfishing is hunting fish underwater with a speargun or pole spear, usually while free-diving.

name: Speartooth shark
fact: The speartooth shark is a rare river shark of northern Australia and Papua New Guinea that moves between rivers, estuaries and the sea.

name: Speckled hind
fact: The speckled hind is a deep-water grouper of the southeastern US, dusted with tiny white spots, so overfished that it is now protected.

name: Spectacled caiman
fact: The spectacled caiman is named for a bony ridge between its eyes that looks like the bridge of a pair of spectacles.

name: Spectacled porpoise
fact: The spectacled porpoise has dark rings around its eyes like glasses and lives in cold sub-Antarctic waters, where it is rarely seen alive.

name: Spectacled sea snake
fact: The spectacled sea snake is a true sea snake that lives in the shallow waters off northern Australia.

name: Spencer Gulf
fact: Spencer Gulf in South Australia was named by Matthew Flinders after George Spencer, the Earl Spencer.

name: Sperm whale
fact: Sperm whales dive over 2 kilometres deep hunting squid and have the largest brain of any animal.

name: Spider crab
fact: European spider crabs pile up in mounds of hundreds during their summer moult and decorate their spiny shells with seaweed.

name: Spine-bellied sea snake
fact: The spine-bellied sea snake is a stout, aggressive sea snake often caught in trawl nets off Australia and Southeast Asia.

name: Spined pygmy shark
fact: The spined pygmy shark is one of the smallest sharks, about 25 centimetres long, and glows from its belly far below the surface.

name: Spinnaker
fact: A spinnaker is a large balloon-like sail used for sailing downwind.

name: Spinner dolphin
fact: Spinner dolphins leap and spin several times in the air, and rest in shallow bays by day after hunting offshore at night.

name: Spinner shark
fact: Spinner sharks charge up through schools of fish and burst from the water spinning, sometimes turning three times in the air.

name: Spiny chromis
fact: The spiny chromis of the Great Barrier Reef is unusual among reef fish in that both parents guard their young for weeks after hatching.

name: Spiny dogfish
fact: Spiny dogfish carry their pups for up to two years, one of the longest pregnancies of any vertebrate.

name: Spiny lobster
fact: Spiny lobsters have no big claws and march across the seabed in single-file lines of dozens during autumn migrations.

name: Spiny starfish
fact: The spiny starfish of European coasts can reach about 70 centimetres across and is armed with rows of blunt spines ringed by tiny pincers.

name: Splendid alfonsino
fact: The splendid alfonsino, kinmedai in Japan, is a red deep-water fish with large golden eyes, served as sushi and sashimi.

name: Splendid garden eel
fact: Splendid garden eels live in colonies in sandy burrows, rising like a field of stalks to catch plankton and sinking back when threatened.

name: Splendid toadfish
fact: The splendid toadfish is found only around Cozumel, Mexico, where it hides under coral ledges and whistles to attract mates.

name: Split
fact: Split in Croatia grew around the palace of the Roman emperor Diocletian, built around AD 300.

name: Sponge
fact: Sponges are the simplest animals, with no organs or nerves, yet a carnivorous sponge was dredged from 9,990 metres in the Philippine Trench.

name: Sponge crab
fact: Sponge crabs cut a living sponge to size and hold it over their backs with their hind legs as a hat that grows with them.

name: Sponge diver
fact: Sponge divers harvested natural sponges from the seabed, a tradition centred on Greece and Florida.

name: SpongeBob SquarePants
fact: SpongeBob SquarePants is the cartoon series created by Stephen Hillenburg, a marine biology teacher, that first aired in 1999.

name: Spot
fact: The spot, a small Atlantic croaker, takes its name from the dark spot behind each gill cover.

name: Spot prawn
fact: The spot prawn is the largest shrimp on the North American Pacific coast and is eaten raw as amaebi in sushi bars.

name: Spotfin butterflyfish
fact: The spotfin butterflyfish is a white and yellow Atlantic butterflyfish that grazes on sponges and small invertebrates.

name: Spotted blue-eye
fact: The spotted blue-eye is a small rainbowfish from northern Australia and New Guinea that stays under about 3.5 centimetres.

name: Spotted boxfish
fact: Male spotted boxfish are blue with gold spots while females are black with white spots, so different that they were once thought to be separate species.

name: Spotted dolphin
fact: Spotted dolphins are born plain and gradually develop their spots as they age.

name: Spotted drum
fact: The spotted drum of the Caribbean has a tall ribbon-like dorsal fin as a juvenile and hides under ledges by day to feed at night.

name: Spotted eagle ray
fact: Spotted eagle rays can leap clear of the water and have a white-spotted back and a whip-like tail armed with venomous spines.

name: Spotted garden eel
fact: The spotted garden eel lives in colonies of hundreds on Indo-Pacific sand slopes, each eel anchored tail-first in its own burrow.

name: Spotted hake
fact: The spotted hake is a small western Atlantic hake marked with a dark spot on its first dorsal fin.

name: Spotted handfish
fact: The spotted handfish of Tasmania walks along the seabed on hand-like fins and is critically endangered, with only a few thousand left.

name: Spotted jelly
fact: Millions of golden jellyfish follow the sun across Palau's Jellyfish Lake each day to feed the algae in their tissues, and their sting is too mild to notice.

name: Spotted mangrove
fact: The spotted mangrove grows on stilt roots along the coasts of northern Australia and the western Pacific.

name: Spotted moray
fact: The spotted moray is a Caribbean and western Atlantic moray whose pale body is covered in small dark spots.

name: Spotted ratfish
fact: The spotted ratfish, a chimaera with rabbit-like teeth and a rat-like tail, carries a venomous spine on its back.

name: Spotted ray
fact: The spotted ray lives on sandy seabeds of the north-east Atlantic and is covered in small dark spots.

name: Spotted scat
fact: The spotted scat is a deep-bodied fish of Indo-Pacific mangroves and estuaries, with dark spots scattered over a golden to silvery body.

name: Spotted scorpionfish
fact: The spotted scorpionfish of the western Atlantic blends into the reef and delivers a painful sting through venomous spines along its back.

name: Spotted sea hare
fact: The spotted sea hare of European coasts is named for its ear-like tentacles, and it can release a cloud of purple ink.

name: Spotted seahorse
fact: The spotted seahorse of the Indo-Pacific is one of the species most heavily traded dried for use in traditional medicine.

name: Spotted seal
fact: Spotted seals breed on the sea ice of the Bering and Okhotsk Seas and are closely related to harbour seals.

name: Spotted seatrout
fact: The spotted seatrout, a drum rather than a trout, makes staccato drumming calls at dusk in spawning season across Gulf of Mexico estuaries.

name: Spotted wobbegong
fact: The spotted wobbegong lies camouflaged on Australian reefs, usually under 2 metres long though reported up to about 3, and has bitten people who stepped on or disturbed it.

name: Sprat
fact: Sprats are tiny herring relatives caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes, smoked whole in Baltic countries and tinned as 'brisling sardines'.

name: Spring tide
fact: Spring tides are the highest and lowest tides, which occur around the new and full Moon when the Sun and Moon pull together.

name: Olive nudibranch
fact: The olive nudibranch eats sea anemones and keeps their stinging cells for its own defence.

name: Spurred mangrove
fact: The bark of the spurred mangrove is rich in tannins and has long been used for dyeing and tanning.

name: Spyglass
fact: A spyglass is a small hand-held telescope, once a standard tool for watching distant ships and coasts.

name: Squalicorax
fact: Squalicorax, the crow shark, was a Cretaceous shark whose serrated teeth are found with the bones of the marine reptiles and other animals it scavenged.

name: Squalodon
fact: Squalodon was an extinct toothed whale of the Oligocene and Miocene with triangular, serrated-edged teeth, and its name means shark tooth.

name: Squaretail coralgrouper
fact: The squaretail coralgrouper gathers in large spawning aggregations at certain places in the Indo-Pacific.

name: Squat lobster
fact: Squat lobsters are flattened crab-like relatives of hermit crabs that tuck their tails under their bodies and swarm on deep-sea coral and vent fields.

name: Squid
fact: Squid swim by jet propulsion, squirting water from a flexible funnel, and some species can launch themselves clear of the surface.

name: Squirrelfish
fact: Squirrelfish are red, big-eyed reef fish that hide in caves by day and come out to hunt at night.

name: Sri Lanka
fact: Sri Lanka is a teardrop-shaped island off the southern tip of India, separated from it by the Palk Strait.

name: SS Arctic
fact: The American paddle steamer Arctic sank in 1854 after colliding with another ship off Newfoundland, and about 350 people died.

name: SS Atlantic
fact: The White Star liner Atlantic struck rocks off Nova Scotia in 1873, and more than 500 people died.

name: SS Bremen
fact: The Bremen was a German liner that took the Blue Riband for the fastest Atlantic crossing in 1929.

name: SS Canberra
fact: The P&O liner Canberra was requisitioned as a troopship during the Falklands War of 1982.

name: SS Central America
fact: The SS Central America, the 'Ship of Gold', sank in an 1857 hurricane with tonnes of California gold, and was found in 1988 about 2,200 metres down off the Carolinas.

name: SS France
fact: The SS France of 1962 was the longest passenger ship in the world for decades, and she later sailed as the cruise ship Norway.

name: SS Gairsoppa
fact: The SS Gairsoppa, torpedoed in 1941, was found in 2011 about 4,700 metres down, and more than 100 tonnes of silver were recovered from it, the deepest such salvage.

name: SS Great Britain
fact: The SS Great Britain, launched in 1843 by Brunel, was the first iron-hulled, propeller-driven ship to cross the Atlantic and is preserved in Bristol.

name: SS Great Eastern
fact: The Great Eastern was Isambard Brunel's enormous iron ship, which in 1866 laid a lasting transatlantic telegraph cable.

name: SS Imperator
fact: The Imperator of 1913 was the largest ship in the world when launched, and she later became Cunard's Berengaria.

name: SS Normandie
fact: The Normandie was a lavish art-deco French liner of 1935 that caught fire and capsized at her New York pier in 1942.

name: SS President Coolidge
fact: The former luxury liner SS President Coolidge sank off Vanuatu in 1942 after striking friendly mines and is now a famous dive site.

name: SS Rex
fact: The Rex was an Italian liner that won the Blue Riband in 1933.

name: SS Rio Grande
fact: The German blockade runner Rio Grande, sunk in 1944, was found in 1996 at 5,762 metres in the South Atlantic and held the record for the deepest shipwreck for decades.

name: SS Savannah
fact: The Savannah, in 1819, was the first steam-powered vessel to cross the Atlantic, though she sailed for most of the voyage.

name: SS Thistlegorm
fact: The SS Thistlegorm, a British freighter sunk in the Red Sea in 1941, still holds motorbikes, trucks and locomotives and is among the most dived wrecks anywhere.

name: SS United States
fact: The SS United States won the Blue Riband for the fastest Atlantic crossing on her maiden voyage in 1952.

name: SS Vaterland
fact: The Vaterland was a giant German liner of 1914 that was seized by the United States in 1917 and renamed Leviathan.

name: SS Waratah
fact: The Waratah, an Australian liner, vanished off South Africa in 1909 with 211 people on board, and no wreck has been confirmed.

name: SS Yongala
fact: The SS Yongala sank in a cyclone off Queensland in 1911 with everyone aboard, and the wreck is now smothered in corals and giant groupers.

name: St. Augustine Lighthouse
fact: The black-and-white spiral-striped St. Augustine Lighthouse in Florida dates from 1874 and has 219 steps to its lantern.

name: St Helena
fact: St Helena is a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic where Napoleon was exiled from 1815 until his death in 1821.

name: St. John's
fact: St. John's, Newfoundland, is the easternmost city in North America and one of the oldest English settlements on the continent.

name: St Kilda
fact: St Kilda is a remote Scottish archipelago with huge seabird colonies, abandoned by its people in 1930.

name: St. Lawrence Seaway
fact: The St. Lawrence Seaway, opened in 1959, lets ocean-going ships travel from the Atlantic into the Great Lakes.

name: Staghorn coral
fact: Staghorn coral grows fast in antler-like branches, but Caribbean staghorn has declined by more than 90 per cent since the 1980s.

name: Staghorn damselfish
fact: The staghorn damselfish is a greenish damselfish with pale bars, named for the staghorn corals it shelters among.

name: Stalked jellyfish
fact: Stalked jellyfish are tiny trumpet-shaped jellyfish that live upside down, glued by a stalk to seaweed and seagrass instead of swimming.

name: Stanchion
fact: A stanchion is an upright post that supports a rail or an awning on a ship's deck.

name: Stand-up paddleboarding
fact: Stand-up paddleboarding is riding a long board while standing and using a single-bladed paddle, a sport that spread from Hawaii.

name: Star coral
fact: Star corals build the massive boulders of Caribbean reefs, and their polyps leave star-shaped cups in the skeleton.

name: Star-sucker pygmy octopus
fact: The star-sucker pygmy octopus is the smallest known octopus, about 2.5 centimetres long and weighing less than a gram.

name: Starboard
fact: Starboard is the right-hand side of a ship when facing forward, from the old steering-board that was fixed on that side.

name: Stargazer
fact: Stargazers bury themselves in sand with only their upward-facing eyes showing, and some species can give an electric shock.

name: Stargazy pie
fact: Stargazy pie is a Cornish pie in which whole pilchards poke their heads through the pastry crust, linked to the village of Mousehole.

name: Starlet sea anemone
fact: The starlet sea anemone is a small estuarine anemone used in research because it can regrow a whole body from a cut piece.

name: Starry flounder
fact: The starry flounder can be left- or right-eyed and is named for the star-shaped spiny scales scattered across its skin.

name: Starry ray
fact: The starry ray, also called the thorny skate, is covered in sharp, star-shaped thorns on its back and tail.

name: Starry triggerfish
fact: The starry triggerfish is a white-spotted Indo-Pacific triggerfish that lives over sandy and rubble bottoms.

name: Steamer Lane
fact: Steamer Lane in Santa Cruz, California, is a long-standing surf spot in the town where Hawaiian princes rode waves in 1885.

name: Steaming
fact: Steaming cooks fish gently over simmering water and is the classic method for whole fish in Cantonese cooking.

name: Stede Bonnet
fact: Stede Bonnet was a wealthy Barbados landowner who became a pirate, earning the nickname the Gentleman Pirate, and was hanged in 1718.

name: Steephead parrotfish
fact: The steephead parrotfish has a steep forehead and strong beak, and it bites away dead coral as it grazes on algae.

name: Stejneger's beaked whale
fact: Stejneger's beaked whale, also called the Bering Sea beaked whale, lives in cold North Pacific waters and often strands in the Aleutian Islands.

name: Steller sea lion
fact: Steller sea lions are the largest sea lions, with bulls reaching about a tonne, and are named after naturalist Georg Steller.

name: Steller's sea cow
fact: Steller's sea cow, an 8-metre relative of the dugong, was hunted to extinction within about 27 years of its discovery in 1741.

name: Steller's sea eagle
fact: Steller's sea eagle, one of the heaviest eagles in the world, catches salmon and cod along the coasts of Kamchatka and winters in Hokkaido.

name: Stellwagen Bank
fact: Stellwagen Bank, a sandy plateau at the mouth of Massachusetts Bay, is a national marine sanctuary famous for its humpback whale watching.

name: Stern
fact: The stern is the back of a ship or boat.

name: Stethacanthus
fact: Stethacanthus was a small shark of about 360 million years ago whose males carried a flat, anvil-shaped dorsal fin topped with tooth-like scales.

name: Stevedore
fact: Stevedores load and unload cargo from ships in port.

name: Stewart Island
fact: Stewart Island, called Rakiura in Maori, is New Zealand's third-largest island and a refuge for kiwi.

name: Stewing
fact: Stewing simmers fish in a flavoured liquid, as in bouillabaisse and other fishermen's stews.

name: Stick chart
fact: The stick charts of the Marshall Islands were made of palm ribs and shells to represent the way ocean swells bend around islands, and navigators learned them on land.

name: Stickleback
fact: Male sticklebacks build a nest from plant material and guard the eggs until they hatch.

name: Stingray
fact: A stingray's venomous barb is a modified scale on its tail, used only in self-defence when the ray is stepped on or threatened.

name: Stinker sponge
fact: The stinker sponge gives off a strong, unpleasant smell when it is out of the water.

name: Stockfish
fact: Stockfish is unsalted cod dried on wooden racks in cold Arctic air, a Norwegian practice around the Lofoten Islands for centuries.

name: Stoker
fact: A stoker shovelled coal into the boilers of a steamship, working in hot and dirty conditions below decks.

name: Stokes's sea snake
fact: Stokes's sea snake is one of the heaviest sea snakes, with a thick body and the longest fangs of any sea snake.

name: Stone crab
fact: Florida stone crabs are fished for their claws alone: a claw is removed and the live crab is returned to the sea to grow a new one.

name: Stonefish
fact: The stonefish is the most venomous fish known, with 13 dorsal spines, and lies half-buried in sand looking exactly like an encrusted rock.

name: Stony coral
fact: Stony corals are the reef builders, each polyp laying down a cup of limestone so that colonies slowly pile up into reefs.

name: Stoplight loosejaw
fact: The stoplight loosejaw shines a red searchlight that most deep-sea animals cannot see, and has a jaw with no floor so it can snap shut faster.

name: Stoplight parrotfish
fact: The stoplight parrotfish of the Caribbean changes from a mottled red-and-brown female phase to a green male with a yellow spot, like a traffic light.

name: Storm surge
fact: A storm surge is a rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by the winds and low pressure of a storm.

name: Stout infantfish
fact: The stout infantfish of the Great Barrier Reef matures at about 7 to 8 millimetres and weighs about a milligram, one of the smallest and lightest vertebrates.

name: Stove-pipe sponge
fact: The stove-pipe sponge grows in long, slender tubes on Caribbean reefs.

name: Strabo Trench
fact: The Strabo Trench is one of the deep trenches of the Hellenic subduction zone south of Crete in the eastern Mediterranean.

name: Straight-nosed pipefish
fact: The straight-nosed pipefish is a thin, snake-like pipefish of European seas, and the male glues the eggs to the outside of his belly.

name: Strait of Belle Isle
fact: The Strait of Belle Isle separates Newfoundland from Labrador and links the Gulf of St Lawrence with the open Atlantic.

name: Strait of Bonifacio
fact: The Strait of Bonifacio separates Corsica from Sardinia and is notorious for strong winds and shipwrecks.

name: Strait of Dover
fact: The Strait of Dover is the narrowest part of the English Channel, about 33 kilometres wide, and one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

name: Strait of Gibraltar
fact: The Strait of Gibraltar joins the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest, between Spain and Morocco.

name: Strait of Hormuz
fact: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and about a fifth of the world's oil passes through it.

name: Strait of Juan de Fuca
fact: The Strait of Juan de Fuca between Washington state and Vancouver Island is named after a Greek sailor, known by his Spanish name Juan de Fuca, who claimed to have found it in 1592.

name: Strait of Kerch
fact: The Strait of Kerch links the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov, and a road and rail bridge across it opened in 2018 and 2019.

name: Strait of Magellan
fact: The Strait of Magellan, named after Ferdinand Magellan who sailed through it in 1520, lets ships pass between the Atlantic and Pacific south of mainland South America.

name: Strait of Malacca
fact: The Strait of Malacca between Malaysia and Sumatra is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, linking the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.

name: Strait of Messina
fact: The Strait of Messina between Sicily and mainland Italy is home to the whirlpools behind the legend of Scylla and Charybdis.

name: Strait of Otranto
fact: The Strait of Otranto between Italy and Albania is the gateway from the Ionian Sea into the Adriatic.

name: Strait of Sicily
fact: The Strait of Sicily lies between Sicily and Tunisia and divides the Mediterranean into its eastern and western basins.

name: Strait of Tiran
fact: The Strait of Tiran guards the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba, and its closure to Israeli shipping in 1967 helped trigger the Six-Day War.

name: Straits of Florida
fact: The Straits of Florida between Florida and Cuba carry the Gulf Stream and heavy shipping out of the Gulf of Mexico.

name: Strap-toothed whale
fact: Male strap-toothed whales, also called Layard's beaked whales, grow two tusks that curl over the upper jaw and stop the mouth opening more than a few centimetres.

name: Strawberry anemone
fact: The strawberry anemone is a red anemone of rocky shores whose green-flecked column looks like a strawberry.

name: Strawberry conch
fact: The strawberry conch is a reef snail with a pink-orange shell opening and eyes on long stalks.

name: Strawberry squid
fact: The strawberry squid has one big eye that looks up for shadows and one small eye that looks down for flashes of light, and skin dotted with photophores.

name: Streaked seerfish
fact: The streaked seerfish is an Indo-Pacific mackerel marked with streaks of dark spots along its sides.

name: Striped bass
fact: Striped bass spawn in rivers such as the Hudson and the tributaries of Chesapeake Bay and spend their adult lives roaming the Atlantic coast.

name: Striped bonito
fact: The striped bonito of the Indo-Pacific is eaten as sashimi in Japan, where it is called hagatsuo.

name: Striped dolphin
fact: Striped dolphins are fast, acrobatic dolphins with blue-black stripes and are the most common dolphin in the Mediterranean.

name: Striped eel catfish
fact: Juvenile striped eel catfish swarm in tight balls on reefs, and each one carries venomous spines that have caused rare human deaths.

name: Striped marlin
fact: The striped marlin hunts in packs off Baja California, where it herds sardine bait balls at high speed and lights up its stripes as it attacks.

name: Striped mullet
fact: Striped mullet wander freely between the sea, estuaries and completely fresh water, but spawn offshore in the open sea.

name: Striped parrotfish
fact: The striped parrotfish is a common Caribbean parrotfish whose young are striped and whose adults are green and purple.

name: Striped Raphael catfish
fact: The striped Raphael catfish, a 'talking catfish', squeaks by grinding its pectoral spines and is armoured with a row of sharp plates along each side.

name: Striped shore crab
fact: The striped shore crab has dark stripes on its square shell and can breathe air as it roams rocks above the waterline.

name: Striped snakehead
fact: The striped snakehead gulps air and can bury itself in mud to survive the dry season.

name: Stromboli
fact: Stromboli is a volcanic island of the Aeolian chain whose volcano has erupted almost continuously for centuries.

name: Sturgeon
fact: Most sturgeons spend their adult lives in the sea or in large lakes and swim up rivers to spawn, and some live for more than 100 years.

name: Subantarctic fur seal
fact: The subantarctic fur seal breeds on remote islands of the southern Indian and Atlantic oceans, such as Amsterdam Island and Gough Island.

name: Subantarctic killer whale
fact: The subantarctic killer whale, or Type D, has a tiny eye patch and a rounded head and was first recognised from a mass stranding in New Zealand in 1955.

name: Submarine
fact: Nuclear submarines can stay underwater for months at a time, limited only by the food they carry for the crew.

name: Sudan
fact: Sudan's only coast is on the Red Sea, where Port Sudan is its main harbour.

name: Suez Canal
fact: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869 and about 193 kilometres long, links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and spares ships the voyage round Africa.

name: Sugar kelp
fact: Sugar kelp has a long, crinkled single blade and gets its name from the sweet white powder, mannitol, that forms on it when dried.

name: Sulphide worm
fact: The sulphide worm chooses to sit in water of about 50 degrees Celsius on vent chimneys, hotter than any other animal has been shown to prefer.

name: Sulu Sea
fact: The Sulu Sea in the south-west Philippines holds the Tubbataha Reefs and is enclosed by Palawan, Borneo and the Sulu Archipelago.

name: Sumatra
fact: Sumatra is the sixth-largest island in the world and is home to wild orangutans, tigers, rhinos and elephants.

name: Sumba
fact: Sumba is an Indonesian island known for its megalithic tombs and its hand-woven ikat textiles.

name: Sumburgh Head Lighthouse
fact: Sumburgh Head Lighthouse at the southern tip of Shetland, built by Robert Stevenson and lit in 1821, overlooks a major seabird colony.

name: Summer flounder
fact: The summer flounder, or fluke, is a left-eyed flatfish prized by anglers on the US east coast and can change colour to match the bottom.

name: Sun coral
fact: Sun coral has no symbiotic algae, so it can grow in dark caves and under piers, opening its bright orange polyps at night to catch plankton.

name: Sunda Shelf
fact: The Sunda Shelf is the drowned extension of mainland South-east Asia, shallow seafloor that linked Borneo, Sumatra and Java to the continent during ice ages.

name: Sunda Strait
fact: The Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra links the Java Sea to the Indian Ocean and holds the volcano Krakatoa.

name: Sundri
fact: The sundri is thought to have given the Sundarbans mangrove forest its name, and it is now an endangered tree.

name: Sunflower sea star
fact: The sunflower sea star has up to 24 arms, speeds along on thousands of tube feet and eats sea urchins, but a wasting disease wiped out most of them after 2013.

name: Sunset Beach
fact: Sunset Beach on Oahu's North Shore is a big, shifting winter wave that hosts the Vans World Cup of Surfing.

name: Supercargo
fact: A supercargo was the merchant's representative aboard a trading ship, in charge of the cargo and its sale.

name: Supergiant amphipod
fact: The supergiant amphipod grows to about 34 centimetres, around ten times the size of most amphipods, and was caught 7,000 metres down in the Kermadec Trench.

name: Supertubos
fact: Supertubos at Peniche in Portugal is a fast, hollow beach break that hosts a World Surf League stop.

name: Surcouf
fact: Surcouf was a giant French submarine of 1929 that carried a seaplane in a hangar, and she was lost in the Caribbean in 1942.

name: Surf clam
fact: The surf clam, hokkigai, is served in sushi with its tip blanched, which turns the foot a bright red.

name: Surf kayaking
fact: Surf kayaking is riding ocean waves in a kayak.

name: Surf lifesaving
fact: Surf lifesaving sport grew from the beach rescue clubs of Australia and tests skills such as swimming, board paddling and rescue.

name: Surf ski paddling
fact: Surf ski paddling uses a long, narrow sit-on-top kayak to race in open sea and ocean swells.

name: Surf smelt
fact: The surf smelt is a small schooling fish that spawns on gravel beaches in the North Pacific and feeds salmon and seabirds.

name: Surfgrass
fact: Surfgrass clings to rocky shores of the north-eastern Pacific and withstands pounding surf rather than rooting in sand.

name: Surfing
fact: Surfing is riding waves on a board, and it developed over centuries among the Polynesians of the Pacific.

name: Surfperch
fact: Surfperches of the North American Pacific coast give birth to fully formed live young, which is unusual for a marine fish.

name: Surfrider Foundation
fact: The Surfrider Foundation was founded by surfers in California in 1984 to protect waves and beaches.

name: Surgeonfish
fact: Surgeonfish are named for the scalpel-like spines at the base of the tail, and they graze algae that would otherwise smother coral.

name: Suriname
fact: Suriname lies on South America's Atlantic coast, and the old centre of its capital, Paramaribo, is a World Heritage Site.

name: Surstromming
fact: Surstromming is a Swedish fermented Baltic herring, famous for the powerful smell that comes out of the tin when opened.

name: Surtsey
fact: Surtsey is a volcanic island off Iceland that rose from the sea in 1963 and has been off limits to all but scientists ever since.

name: Suruga Bay
fact: Suruga Bay is the deepest bay in Japan and is known for the Japanese spider crab.

name: Suruga Trough
fact: The Suruga Trough off the coast of Shizuoka in Japan forms the north-eastern end of the Nankai Trough.

name: Sushi
fact: Sushi is a Japanese dish of vinegared rice served with raw or cooked fish and other toppings.

name: Sustainable Fisheries Partnership
fact: The Sustainable Fisheries Partnership works with the seafood industry to improve how fisheries are managed.

name: Suva
fact: Suva on the island of Viti Levu is the capital and largest port of Fiji.

name: Sverdrup
fact: The sverdrup is the unit used for ocean currents, equal to one million cubic metres of water moving each second.

name: Swamp eel
fact: The Asian swamp eel breathes air, burrows into mud when ponds dry out, and has become an invader of Florida and Georgia wetlands.

name: Sweetlips
fact: Sweetlips are reef fish named for their thick, fleshy lips, and their juveniles often look nothing like the adults.

name: Swell
fact: Swell consists of long, regular waves that have travelled out of the storm that made them, sometimes for thousands of miles.

name: Swell shark
fact: The swell shark glows green under blue light and can gulp water to double its size and wedge itself into a crevice when threatened.

name: Swimming
fact: Swimming in the sea is one of the oldest water sports, and open-water swimming events cover distances from a few hundred metres to marathon crossings.

name: Swimming eolid
fact: The swimming eolid houses algae in its feathery gills and can swim by wriggling its body.

name: Sword Beach
fact: Sword Beach was the easternmost of the D-Day landing beaches, assigned to British forces on 6 June 1944.

name: Swordfish
fact: Swordfish slash at squid with a flat bill and are among the fastest fish in the sea; their meaty steaks are eaten worldwide and served raw as mekajiki in Japan.

name: Swordtail
fact: The male swordtail grows a long blade from the bottom of its tail that females prefer longer, a classic example of sexual selection.

name: Swordtip squid
fact: The swordtip squid is a Pacific squid caught for food in Japan and elsewhere in East Asia.

name: Sydney
fact: Sydney grew around Port Jackson, where the First Fleet landed in 1788 to found the first British colony in Australia.

name: Sydney rock oyster
fact: The Sydney rock oyster has been farmed in New South Wales estuaries since the 1870s, making it Australia's oldest aquaculture industry.

name: Sylvia Earle
fact: Sylvia Earle, nicknamed Her Deepness, set a record in 1979 by walking the sea floor at 381 metres in a pressurised suit and has spent thousands of hours underwater.

name: Symphony of the Seas
fact: Symphony of the Seas, built in 2018, is a Royal Caribbean cruise ship of the Oasis class.

name: Synechococcus
fact: Synechococcus is a tiny photosynthetic bacterium, only about a micrometre wide, that is abundant across the oceans.

name: Synodontis catfish
fact: Synodontis catfish of Africa are called squeakers because they chirp by rubbing their pectoral spines; the featherfin squeaker is an aquarium favourite.

name: Table Bay
fact: Table Bay is the Atlantic bay beneath Table Mountain at Cape Town, with Robben Island at its mouth.

name: Table coral
fact: Table coral grows outward in broad, flat plates that shade the reef below and give small fish a roof to hide under.

name: Tadpole fish
fact: The tadpole fish is a small, big-headed relative of the cod found on rocky coasts of the north-east Atlantic.

name: Taffrail
fact: The taffrail is the rail around the stern of a ship, and a ship's log was often streamed from here.

name: Tahiti
fact: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, a volcanic peak ringed by reef, where Captain Cook observed the transit of Venus in 1769.

name: Taillight shark
fact: The taillight shark is a rarely seen, small deep-water shark with light-producing organs, and only a handful of specimens are known.

name: Taimen
fact: The taimen of Siberia and Mongolia is the largest salmonid in the world, reaching about 2 metres and living for more than 50 years.

name: Taiwan
fact: Taiwan is an island off the coast of China, and its eastern shore faces the open Pacific.

name: Taiwan Strait
fact: The Taiwan Strait separates Taiwan from mainland China and is about 130 kilometres wide at its narrowest.

name: Takoyaki
fact: Takoyaki are Japanese balls of batter with a piece of octopus inside, a street food that comes from Osaka.

name: Talcahuano
fact: Talcahuano in central Chile is a major naval base and fishing port on the Bay of Concepcion.

name: Tall-stilt mangrove
fact: The tall-stilt mangrove is a major source of timber and charcoal in the mangrove forests of South-East Asia.

name: Tambaqui
fact: The tambaqui follows the flooded forest in the wet season and cracks fallen fruits and nuts with its strong, flat teeth.

name: Verco's nudibranch
fact: Verco's nudibranch is a brightly coloured sea slug of southern Australian coasts that feeds on bryozoans.

name: Tampa Bay
fact: Tampa Bay is Florida's largest open-water estuary, on the Gulf of Mexico.

name: Tanaid
fact: Tanaids are tiny, shrimp-like crustaceans that build tubes in the mud and are among the commonest animals in deep trench sediments.

name: Tangaroa
fact: Tangaroa is the Maori and wider Polynesian god of the sea, and in Maori tradition the fish and sea creatures are his children.

name: Tangier
fact: Tangier is a Moroccan port at the western entrance of the Strait of Gibraltar, where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.

name: Tanya Streeter
fact: Tanya Streeter, a freediver from the Cayman Islands, set a no-limits world record of 160 metres in 2002.

name: Tanzania
fact: Tanzania's Indian Ocean coast includes Dar es Salaam and the islands of Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia.

name: Tape seagrass
fact: Tape seagrass is among the largest seagrasses of the Indo-Pacific, with ribbon-like leaves that can be a metre or more long.

name: Tara Oceans expedition
fact: The Tara Oceans expedition of 2009 to 2013 sailed the schooner Tara around the world to sample plankton.

name: Tarakihi
fact: Tarakihi is a silvery, banded fish of New Zealand's coastal waters and one of the country's most commonly eaten fish.

name: Tarpon
fact: Tarpon gulp air into a swim bladder that works like a lung, and young tarpon grow up in brackish and freshwater backwaters before moving out to sea.

name: Tarragona
fact: Tarragona in Spain was the Roman city of Tarraco, and its Roman ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Tasman beaked whale
fact: The Tasman beaked whale keeps a full set of functional teeth in both jaws, unlike most beaked whales.

name: Tasman Sea
fact: The Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand is named after the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, who sailed it in 1642, and is nicknamed the Ditch.

name: Tasman's voyage of 1642
fact: Abel Tasman's 1642 voyage was the first European sighting of Tasmania and New Zealand.

name: Tasmanian giant crab
fact: The Tasmanian giant crab can weigh more than 13 kilograms and has one huge claw; it lives on the edge of the continental shelf off southern Australia.

name: Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish
fact: The Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish is the largest freshwater invertebrate on Earth, once reaching about 6 kilograms, and can live for about 40 years.

name: Tasselled wobbegong
fact: The tasselled wobbegong has a fringe of branching skin lobes around its head, and one was photographed on the Great Barrier Reef with a whole bamboo shark head-first in its jaws.

name: Tataki
fact: Tataki is a Japanese method of searing fish on the outside, leaving it raw inside, and slicing it, famously done with bonito.

name: Tauranga
fact: The Port of Tauranga in New Zealand is the largest export port in the country by volume.

name: Tautog
fact: The tautog, or blackfish, is a chunky wrasse of the US east coast that sleeps so soundly on the bottom at night that divers can pick it up.

name: Tawny nurse shark
fact: The tawny nurse shark is a docile Indo-Pacific reef shark that sucks prey from crevices and rests in groups in reef caves.

name: Tea mangrove
fact: The tea mangrove, found on the Pacific coast of the Americas, bears unusually large flowers for a mangrove.

name: Teahupo'o
fact: Teahupo'o in Tahiti breaks as a thick, heavy wave over a shallow reef and hosted the surfing events at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

name: Technical diving
fact: Technical diving is scuba diving beyond the usual recreational limits, using special gas mixtures and staged decompression.

name: Jaffa
fact: Jaffa is one of the oldest ports in the world and now forms part of Tel Aviv.

name: Telescope octopus
fact: The telescope octopus is a see-through deep-sea octopus with tubular eyes on stalks that point upward to spot prey against the faint light.

name: Telescopefish
fact: The telescopefish has forward-pointing tubular eyes like a pair of binoculars and can swallow prey longer than itself.

name: Temnodontosaurus
fact: Temnodontosaurus was a large Early Jurassic ichthyosaur, around nine metres long, with some of the biggest eyes of any known vertebrate.

name: Tempura
fact: Tempura is Japanese battered and deep-fried seafood or vegetables, a technique that Portuguese traders brought to Japan in the sixteenth century.

name: Tench
fact: The tench, a slimy olive fish of still European waters, was once believed to heal other fish that rubbed against it.

name: Tennessee Aquarium
fact: The Tennessee Aquarium in Chattanooga opened in 1992 and was the largest freshwater aquarium in the world at the time.

name: Teppanyaki
fact: Teppanyaki is Japanese cooking on a flat iron griddle, often with seafood like prawns and scallops.

name: Tern
fact: Terns hover over the water and then plunge head-first to seize small fish just below the surface.

name: Terra Nova expedition
fact: The Terra Nova expedition of 1910 to 1913 reached the South Pole, but Scott and his four companions died on the return march.

name: Tethys
fact: Tethys was a Titan sea goddess in Greek myth, wife of Oceanus and mother of the river gods and the Oceanids.

name: Texel
fact: Texel is the largest of the Dutch Wadden Sea islands.

name: Textile cone
fact: The textile cone is a cone snail patterned like woven cloth that harpoons its prey with venom and can be dangerous to people.

name: Thailand
fact: Thailand has a west coast on the Andaman Sea, which is part of the Indian Ocean, as well as a coast on the Gulf of Thailand.

name: Thalassa
fact: Thalassa was the Greek primordial spirit of the sea, whose name is the ancient Greek word for sea.

name: Thalassia hemprichii
fact: Thalassia hemprichii is the Indo-Pacific cousin of turtle grass, with sickle-shaped leaves grazed by green turtles and dugongs.

name: Thalassodendron ciliatum
